P2A00.d: Sensor 1 on bank 1 is the oxygen sensor ahead of the catalytic converter that the engine control module relies on for mixture feedback. P2A00 is a plausibility fault: a signal is present but does not behave the way fuel control expects.
s: Check engine light on
Engine runs in open loop, fuel consumption rises
Uneven idle or hesitation
Failed emissions inspection
c: Sensor aged or poisoned (oil ash, silicone, coolant), signal too weak or sluggish
Leak in intake manifold or exhaust ahead of the sensor distorts the oxygen reading
High resistance or corrosion in signal, reference or heater wiring
Fuel delivery or injector fault the sensor correctly reports but fuel control cannot correct

P2A01.d: Sensor 2 on bank 1 sits behind the catalytic converter and mainly serves to judge how well the converter stores oxygen. Ford uses P2A01 for a signal that is out of range on the low side: on petrol engines with certain Continental control modules from 2011, and still in its 2020–2023 summary, a reading under −0.2 V lasting 10 s sets the code, usually because signal and return wires are swapped or the sensor is worn.
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor stays incomplete
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Engine oil or moisture in the sensor connector (Mazda CX-9 connector C-34)
Signal and return wires swapped, e.g. after a sensor replacement
On diesels, oxygen output of the second NOx sensor drifting

P2A02.d: Sensor 3 on bank 1 follows a second converter or, on diesels, a further aftertreatment stage. GM is the only maker found that documents P2A02: in its 2025 diesel tables the oxygen value of the third NOx sensor is held against that of sensor 2 while the engine runs at full load, and a gap of more than 6 % in either direction in 120 of 240 samples sets a two-trip Type B fault.
s: Check engine light on
Aftertreatment monitor does not complete
No noticeable effect on driving in most cases
c: Oxygen output of the third NOx or oxygen sensor drifting with age
Exhaust leak between sensor 2 and sensor 3 lets outside air in
Sensor coated with soot, ash or urea deposits

P2A03.d: Bank 2 is the cylinder bank that does not contain cylinder 1, so P2A03 only occurs on V or flat engines; sensor 1 is the oxygen sensor ahead of that bank's converter used for fuel control. The fault is the bank-2 counterpart of P2A00: the sensor delivers a signal, yet fuel control cannot close the loop with it or keep it closed.
s: Check engine light on
Higher fuel consumption
Rough idle or exhaust odour
Failed emissions inspection
c: Bank 2 front sensor aged or poisoned, too slow to reach closed loop
Sensor heater weak or wiring with high resistance, sensor stays too cold
Exhaust leak at the bank 2 manifold ahead of the sensor
Real mixture problem on bank 2 (injector, vacuum leak) the sensor reports correctly

P2A04.d: Sensor 2 on bank 2 is the oxygen sensor behind that bank's catalytic converter, used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Ford documents P2A04 together with P2A01 for certain Continental control modules on petrol engines from 2011, and again in its 2020–2023 summary: a rear-sensor voltage that stays below −0.2 V over 10 s sets the code – a value an intact switching sensor should not produce, normally point
s: Check engine light on
Often stored together with a stuck-lean code for the same sensor
Catalyst monitor of bank 2 not ready
c: Oil in the sensor connector from a leaking oil pressure switch (Mazda CX-9)
Signal and return wires swapped or sensors of both banks plugged in crosswise

P2A05.d: P2A05 refers to the third oxygen sensor on bank 2, mounted behind a further converter or aftertreatment stage of a V or flat engine. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Readiness for the catalyst or aftertreatment monitor missing
Usually no change in driving behaviour
c: Third sensor on bank 2 drifting or slow with age
Exhaust leak in the pipe between sensor 2 and sensor 3
Damaged or heat-affected wiring under the vehicle

P2A06.d: P2A06 means the switching oxygen sensor ahead of the converter on bank 1 is delivering a voltage below zero. A zirconia sensor generates its voltage from the oxygen difference between exhaust gas and reference air, normally about 0.1–0.9 V; a negative value means the exhaust side looks richer in oxygen than the reference side, or the polarity at the module is reversed.
s: Check engine light on
Mixture control falls back to open loop, consumption rises
Possible rough idle or poor emissions result
c: Cracked ceramic element, for instance after water shock or impact
Signal and signal-return wires swapped at connector or after a repair
Reference air path of the sensor contaminated by oil, sealant or water

P2A07.d: Sensor 2 on bank 1 is the switching oxygen sensor behind the converter; P2A07 says its output has dropped below zero volts. Because the voltage comes from the oxygen difference across the zirconia element, a negative value points to reversed signal and return wires, a contaminated reference air path or a cracked element.
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst monitor of bank 1 not ready
Usually no noticeable change while driving
c: Signal and return wires swapped, e.g. after fitting a universal sensor
Sensor degraded or reference air contaminated

P2A08.d: P2A08 is the negative-voltage fault of the third oxygen sensor on bank 1, which sits behind a second converter or another aftertreatment stage. Such a sensor is normally a zirconia switching type whose output should stay above zero; an intact, correctly wired sensor does not deliver a negative reading in normal operation, so the code suggests swapped leads, a short between the signal return and another circuit, or a
s: Check engine light on
Converter monitor readiness missing
Normal driving behaviour in most cases
c: Signal return shorted to another circuit or leads swapped
Fault in the module's sensor input stage

P2A09.d: P2A09 concerns the pre-converter oxygen sensor on bank 2, so it only arises on two-bank engines that use switching sensors ahead of the converters. The module reads a voltage below zero from it.
s: Check engine light on
Higher fuel consumption due to open-loop operation of bank 2
Possible rough idle
c: Cracked element in the bank 2 front sensor
Signal wires swapped or bank 1 and bank 2 connectors interchanged
Reference air path contaminated by oil, water or sealant

P2A0A.d: Engines with two intake manifold pressure sensors call the second one sensor B; in GM's tables for the Corvette's LT6 V8 it measures the manifold pressure of bank 2, next to the bank-1 sensor that uses the familiar P0105–P0109 codes. P2A0A is the general circuit fault of sensor B, meant for cases where the module sees a circuit problem without sorting it into low, high or intermittent.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running or hesitation
Possible reduced power
c: Loose connector, corroded terminal or damaged wire at sensor B
5 V reference shared with other sensors pulled down

P2A0B.d: P2A0B means the MAP B signal stays inside its electrical range but does not fit the operating state. GM documents it for the Corvette's LT6 V8, where sensor B reads the bank-2 manifold pressure, with several checks: before the engine turns, the raw reading has to agree with ambient pressure within a few kPa, otherwise one trip and 5 s are enough; with the engine running it is held against a modelled manifold pressure
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation or uneven idle
Mixture or load faults on bank 2
c: Air leak in the bank 2 intake behind the throttle
Sensor port blocked by deposits or frozen condensate
Sensor B drifting so that its reading no longer matches ambient or model

P2A0C.d: P2A0C reports that the MAP B signal voltage is too low. Manifold pressure sensors are usually three-wire parts fed from a 5 V reference; a signal close to zero means a broken reference or signal wire, a ground short or a dead sensor, because even deep vacuum would not pull a healthy sensor down that far.
s: Check engine light on
Sluggish response or rough running
Possible reduced engine power
c: 5 V reference or signal wire open

P2A0D.d: P2A0D is the high-voltage counterpart: the MAP B signal sits close to the reference voltage. Typical reasons are an open ground wire, a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or a sensor that has failed internally.
s: Check engine light on
Rough running or hesitation
Possible limited power
c: Sensor ground wire open or connector not seated
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage

P2A0E.d: P2A0E flags a MAP B signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing for good. No manufacturer documents P2A0E publicly; GM's LT6 tables, the only public description of a sensor B, cover just its low, high and plausibility faults.
s: Intermittent stumble or hesitation
Fault comes and goes, warning light depending on manufacturer
c: Loose or widened terminal in the sensor B connector
Harness chafing on engine parts, intermittent short or open
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

P2A0F.d: A fuel supply heater warms the fuel on its way to the engine. On diesels it sits at the filter so that paraffin wax cannot block it in frost; on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends heated fuel eases cold starts, as a Kia patent with a heated ethanol path to a separate cold-start injector shows.
s: Hard starting in cold weather
Rough running or power loss in severe frost
Fault code stored, warning light depending on manufacturer
c: Heating element burnt out or with too high resistance
Heater relay, fuse or supply wiring not delivering full voltage
Fuel temperature sensor reports wrongly, so the heating effect seems absent

P2A10.d: The downstream oxygen sensor of bank 2, behind that bank's converter, is reporting a negative voltage. Bank 2 only exists on V and flat engines.
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst monitor of bank 2 not ready
No change in driving behaviour
c: Signal and return wires swapped, e.g. on a spliced universal sensor
Cracked ceramic of the bank 2 downstream sensor

P2A11.d: P2A11 is assigned to bank 2's third oxygen sensor, located after a second converter or additional aftertreatment of a two-bank engine, and says its signal has gone negative. For an intact, properly connected zirconia sensor that is not a normal state; likely explanations are reversed leads, a short within the harness or a cracked sensing element.
s: Check engine light on
Dependent catalyst or aftertreatment monitor incomplete
c: Leads swapped or harness short near the exhaust
Fault in the module's sensor input

P2A12.d: The injection pump fuel metering codes cover electrically controlled actuators that decide how much fuel a diesel pump delivers – on distributor pumps the quantity solenoid, on common rail usually the inlet metering unit on the high-pressure pump, which a Bosch patent describes together with its flushing line. Actuators A and B have their own code groups (P0251 ff., P0256 ff.); C continues the series for pumps or eng
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Hard starting or stalling
c: Open circuit or poor contact in the actuator C wiring or connector
Metering actuator C coil failed or valve sticking
Dirt or water in the fuel jamming the metering valve

P2A13.d: P2A13 flags metering element C of a diesel injection system as implausible: its circuit is electrically intact, yet the quantity or pressure it is supposed to produce does not follow the engine control module's command. The letter C stands for a third element – a further metering valve, a cam-driven pump plunger or a unit injector with its own solenoid.
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power, especially under load
Engine power derated by the control module
c: Fault in the high-pressure system (leak, relief valve, low-pressure supply) that the element cannot compensate
Worn or sticking metering element C (valve, plunger or cam lobe)
Outdated engine control software or calibration

P2A14.d: P2A14 reports that the signal in the drive circuit of fuel metering element C has fallen below its expected window. In practice the control module sees too little voltage or current on that output, as happens when the line touches ground or, depending on the driver design, an open wire.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Rough running or misfire-like shaking
c: Control wire of element C chafed through and shorted to ground
Broken wire or corroded, loose connector pin in the element C circuit
Coil of metering element C open or shorted to its housing
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2A15.d: With P2A15 the engine control module finds the circuit of metering element C reading too high: voltage where the driver expects a pulled-down line, or a current beyond the limit. Causes are a chafed wire touching battery voltage, a short between windings inside the actuator, or a failing output stage.
s: Check engine light on
Strongly limited power and accelerator response
Engine may stall or refuse to start
c: Shorted turns in the coil of metering element C drawing excess current
Control wire of element C shorted to battery voltage
Output stage in the engine control module no longer switching correctly

P2A16.d: P2A16 is the umbrella code for fuel metering element D, used when the control module registers a malfunction of that element without assigning it to the more specific plausibility, low or high codes (P2A17–P2A19). The D series only makes sense on systems with at least four individually controlled metering elements, such as engines whose camshaft drives several pumping units.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Hard starting or uneven running
c: Wiring or connector fault in the circuit of element D
Metering element D (valve, pumping unit or injector solenoid) defective
Engine control module fault or software error

P2A17.d: P2A17 means fuel metering element D is not delivering what the control module commands, although its circuit shows no electrical fault. Volvo and Mack document the code for their 11 and 13 litre engines (including Mack MP7/MP8) built to the US17 emissions level, together with P0257 and P2A1F.
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power
Further rail pressure codes stored at the same time
c: Injector lobe turned on the assembled camshaft (Volvo/Mack US17)
Rail pressure problem such as an internal leak or poor low-pressure supply
Worn pumping injector or rocker of element D
Outdated diagnostic software leading to wrong test results

P2A18.d: P2A18 indicates a low reading in the control circuit of metering element D: the module detects that the output stays near ground or carries too little current. Typical triggers are a short to ground in the harness, a corroded connector pin or, with low-side drivers, an interrupted lead.
s: Check engine light on
Limited power or limp mode
Fault may come and go with vibration or moisture
c: Harness of element D shorted to ground
Corroded or spread connector pin at element D
Interrupted lead on the switched side of element D
Defective driver in the engine control module

P2A19.d: P2A19 is stored when the circuit of metering element D reads high – for instance a control line shorted to battery voltage, an actuator coil with shorted turns pulling excessive current, or a driver that no longer switches off. The fault is electrical; whether the element would still meter correctly cannot be judged until the circuit is repaired.
s: Warning lamp on immediately
Severe power reduction
Possible stalling or no start
c: Control line of element D shorted to battery voltage
Actuator coil of element D with shorted turns
Output stage in the control module stuck switched on

P2A1A.d: P2A1A covers fuel metering element E in general: the engine control module has seen a malfunction of that element but files it under none of the more specific codes for plausibility (P2A1B) or low and high signal (P2A1C, P2A1D). A fifth separately driven element is rare; it presupposes engines that meter fuel per cylinder or per pumping unit.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Uneven idle
c: Wiring or connector fault at metering element E
Metering element E or its solenoid defective

P2A1B.d: P2A1B reports that metering element E works electrically but its result is off: the pressure build-up or quantity attributed to it deviates from what was commanded, or its correction values sit at the limit. How a control module rates this is not published; rail pressure and fuel correction are the obvious inputs.
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power under load
Longer cranking before start
c: Worn cam lobe, plunger or valve of metering element E
Insufficient low-pressure supply or clogged filter

P2A1C.d: P2A1C is set when the drive circuit of the fifth metering element, E, reads below its permitted range. On solenoid-operated pump valves and unit injectors, a wire grounded against the engine block, water in a connector or a broken lead on the ground-switched side are typical.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Rough running
c: Wire of element E rubbing on the engine block and grounded
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of element E
Broken lead on the ground-switched side

P2A1D.d: P2A1D tells that metering element E's circuit sits above its plausible range. Faults that cause it include a lead rubbing through onto a powered wire, moisture bridging pins, an actuator winding shorted internally so that current climbs, or a defective output stage in the control unit.
s: Check engine light on
Marked power limitation
Engine may cut out
c: Internal winding short in metering element E
Lead of element E chafed onto a powered wire or pins bridged by moisture
Defective output stage in the control unit

P2A1E.d: P2A1E is the general fault of the sixth fuel metering element, F – the last letter of this code family. The control module stores it for a failure of that element that it cannot pin down as a plausibility (P2A1F), low (P2A20) or high (P2A21) fault.
s: Check engine light on
Derated power
Uneven running
c: Wiring or connector fault in the circuit of element F
Pumping unit, valve or injector solenoid of element F defective

P2A1F.d: P2A1F says that metering element F does not reach its target although its wiring checks out. Volvo and Mack document it for their US17-generation 11 and 13 litre engines, alongside P0257 and P2A17.
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power
Rail pressure codes stored alongside
c: Injector lobe spun on the assembled camshaft (Volvo/Mack US17)
Low-pressure supply too weak or a leak in the rail system
Worn pumping injector of element F
Outdated workshop software misleading the guided test

P2A20.d: P2A20 is the low-signal fault of metering element F: the module measures a voltage or current on that drive line that is lower than the switching state allows. Shorts to ground, broken conductors on low-side switched circuits and connectors pushed out of their housing are the usual suspects.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Rough idle
c: Drive line of element F shorted to ground
Terminal pushed out of the connector housing or broken conductor
Open coil in metering element F

P2A21.d: P2A21 marks a high reading in the circuit of the sixth metering element, F. The control module sees battery potential on the line or a current exceeding the driver limit – for instance when the harness rubs through onto a supply wire or the actuator coil is partly short-circuited.
s: Check engine light on
Severely limited power and throttle response
Possible stalling
c: Partly short-circuited coil of metering element F
Harness of element F chafed onto a supply wire
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P2A22.d: P2A22 covers the drive circuit of shutoff valve B, the electric lock on a further gas cylinder of a multi-tank CNG or LPG installation, when the module finds no current path at all. A broken lead, a loose plug or a burnt-out coil are the usual findings.
s: Check engine light
Noticeably shorter range on gas
Gas left in one cylinder after the others are empty
c: Broken lead or disconnected plug at the valve on tank B
Burnt-out solenoid coil of valve B
Corroded terminals in the valve connector

P2A23.d: P2A23 is stored when valve B is switched on electrically, but the gas system does not react as if that cylinder had opened. Software can only judge this from pressure: after the command, the reading downstream of the tank should rise, and a tank B pressure sensor, where fitted, should fall while gas is being used.
s: Check engine light
Tank B stays full while the others empty
Reduced range on gas
c: Armature of valve B jammed closed, e.g. by debris
Manual valve on tank B left closed
Tank or line pressure sensor reporting the response wrongly

P2A24.d: P2A24 means the alternative fuel module sees the control line of shutoff valve B sitting too low. TransEco Energy, which converts trucks to CNG, assigns it in the fault table of its AFCM v1.4 to a lead shorted to ground or open, lights the MIL on dedicated and bi-fuel systems alike and does not force a fallback.
s: Check engine light
Gas from tank B unavailable, range reduced
c: Control wire of valve B chafed through to ground at a tank bracket
Open lead, which the TransEco module reports under this code
Shorted turns in the coil of valve B

P2A25.d: P2A25 reports a voltage on the control circuit of tank valve B that is higher than the module expects, mostly because the wire touches a battery feed. TransEco Energy's fault table names a short to power as the cause, turns on the MIL and lets the gas system carry on.
s: Check engine light
Tank B may stay open with the engine off
c: Control wire of valve B touching a battery feed
Output stage for valve B in the module stuck on
Wiring mistake during conversion or repair

P2A26.d: P2A26 is the open-circuit code for shutoff valve C, the solenoid on yet another gas cylinder. The module drives the coil and finds that no current flows, so the coil, its plug or the lead to it is interrupted.
s: Check engine light
Gas in cylinder C cannot be used
c: Interrupted lead or unplugged connector at valve C
Faulty driver for valve C in the control module

P2A27.d: P2A27 points to valve C: electrically commanded, yet apparently still shut. With several cylinders on one manifold, a single tank that stays isolated rarely stops the engine; the others keep supplying gas, and the fault appears as shorter range or a cylinder that never empties.
s: Check engine light
Cylinder C never empties
Shorter range on gas
c: Sticking or contaminated armature in valve C
Hand valve on cylinder C closed
Coil voltage too low because of a poor feed or ground

P2A28.d: P2A28 tells that the control line of shutoff valve C reads too low. In TransEco Energy's AFCM table the cause is a lead to ground or an interruption; the MIL lights in both dedicated and bi-fuel conversions, and the vehicle continues without a forced change of fuel.
s: Check engine light
Cylinder C not used or not shut off correctly
c: Insulation of the valve C wire worn through at a clamp
Interrupted lead, reported here by some modules
Coil of valve C shorted internally

P2A29.d: P2A29 sets when the drive circuit of shutoff valve C sits at a high level, as with a wire touching battery voltage or a driver stage inside the module that will not switch off. TransEco's table for its AFCM v1.4 gives a short to power as the cause, with the MIL on and gas operation maintained.
s: Check engine light
Cylinder C not sealed when the engine is off
c: Valve C control wire in contact with battery voltage
Driver stage for valve C will not switch off
Valve C wired to a permanent feed after a conversion

P2A2A.d: P2A2A marks an interrupted control circuit at shutoff valve D, which only exists on installations with four or more gas cylinders, mostly commercial trucks, vans and buses. When the module energizes the coil and measures no current, it stores this code.
s: Check engine light
Reduced usable gas quantity
c: Break in the branch of the harness leading to valve D
Common supply via relay or inertia switch interrupted (several valve codes at once)

P2A2B.d: P2A2B is the functional fault of valve D: the module has commanded it open, but the pressure picture suggests that cylinder D is not contributing gas. Bus builder New Flyer gives figures for the scale involved: its tanks hold between 1,375 and 24,800 kPa, while the regulated side should read 648 to 827 kPa once the engine runs.
s: Check engine light
Tank D stays at full pressure
Reduced range on gas
c: Weak coil that no longer pulls the armature
Hand valve on tank D closed after service

P2A2C.d: P2A2C records too low a level on the control wire of shutoff valve D. TransEco Energy treats it in its AFCM v1.4 fault list as a short to ground or open circuit and switches on the MIL while letting gas operation continue; P2A1C is printed beside it as an alternative number.
s: Check engine light
Gas from tank D not available
c: Valve D wire grounded at a chafe point on the cylinder rack
Salt corrosion in the valve D connector

P2A2D.d: P2A2D reports excessive voltage on the control circuit of shutoff valve D. The AFCM fault list from TransEco Energy names a short to power, lights the MIL and keeps the gas system in service; P2A1D stands next to it.
s: Check engine light
Tank D possibly open with the engine off
c: Valve D lead pinched against a supply cable
Module output for valve D stays on
Error while wiring a conversion kit

P2A2E.d: P2A2E is the open-circuit fault for shutoff valve E, the last letter of this series, so it only applies to systems with at least five gas cylinders, such as transit buses or heavy trucks. The module notices that the coil draws no current when commanded.
s: Check engine light
Gas in cylinder E remains unused
c: Valve E connector not plugged in after tank work
Broken wire in the harness branch to tank E

P2A2F.d: P2A2F signals that valve E was energized but the system did not see the expected gas flow from that cylinder. No manufacturer publishes this code or its test conditions; CARB only requires output components to be checked for a proper reaction to commands.
s: Check engine light
Cylinder E does not empty
Fault appears mainly after cold or weak-battery starts
c: Voltage drop during cranking, coil cannot lift the armature
Manual valve on cylinder E closed

P2A30.d: P2A30 sets when the control circuit of shutoff valve E reads low. TransEco Energy's AFCM v1.4 table names a short to ground or an open lead as the reason and keeps both dedicated and bi-fuel vehicles running, MIL on; P2A20 is listed beside it.
s: Check engine light
Gas from tank E not usable
c: Control lead of valve E touching ground
Shared ground or connector near the module (several low codes together)

P2A31.d: P2A31 closes the shutoff valve series with the high fault on valve E: the module measures voltage on the control wire where none should be. TransEco names a short to power and lights the MIL while the gas system continues; it prints P2A21 beside the code.
s: Check engine light
Cylinder E not locked when it should be
c: Valve E wire shorted to a voltage source
Driver for valve E in the module stuck on
Valve E fed from a wrong circuit after an upfit

P2A32.d: Gas installations that carry a separate control unit for the gas side, the AFCM, may feed that unit through a relay whose coil is switched by a driver stage. P2A32 means this coil circuit shows no current path: the driver output sees an open line, a missing plug or a burnt coil.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode cannot be selected, vehicle stays on petrol
Dedicated gas engine: no start
c: Broken control wire or unplugged relay socket
Blown fuse in the coil feed of the relay
Output driver in the controlling module faulty

P2A33.d: P2A33 concerns the control line that grounds the coil of the relay supplying the gas control module. Low means this line already sits near zero volts while the driver is switched off.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Battery flat after the vehicle has been parked
Gas module stays active after ignition off
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted turns in the relay coil
Moisture in the relay socket bridging to ground

P2A34.d: With P2A34 the coil control line of the gas module power relay stays at high voltage even when the driver tries to pull it to ground. Either the wire has contact with a battery-fed circuit, or the coil draws so much current that the driver shuts itself off for protection.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation unavailable, bi-fuel vehicle runs on petrol only
Dedicated gas engine: cranks but does not start
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Relay coil with too low resistance overloading the driver
Wrong relay type fitted after a repair

P2A35.d: Besides driving the relay coil, a control module can read back the voltage behind the relay contacts to confirm that power actually arrives. P2A35 is the general fault of this feedback line for the relay that supplies the gas control module, without a statement about too low or too high.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Often no drivability change
Occasional fallback to petrol if the supply really drops
c: Sense wire open or pin backed out
Blown fuse between relay contact and sense point
Corroded terminals in relay socket or module plug

P2A36.d: P2A36 is set when the relay feeding the gas control module has been commanded on, yet the voltage read back after its contacts stays too low. Burnt or pitted contacts, a high-resistance joint, a grounded sense wire or a blown fuse in the switched path all lead there, as does a weak battery during cranking.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode drops out, bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol
Communication fault with the gas module stored as well
c: Blown fuse in the switched supply
Weak battery or poor main ground

P2A37.d: Here the read-back line of the gas module supply relay carries voltage at a moment when it should not: the relay is commanded off, yet power is still present behind its contacts. A welded contact pair is the main suspect, followed by a sense wire touching another live circuit.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Battery drained after standing
Relay clicks are missing at ignition off
c: Sense wire shorted to another live circuit
Miswired retrofit gas installation feeding voltage back

P2A38.d: P2A38 reports that the lead carrying positive current control for bank 1's third oxygen sensor has no continuity. That sensor sits behind a second converter or a later aftertreatment stage, and the code only makes sense where this position carries a wide-band probe: through this lead (pin APE/IP on a Bosch LSU 4.9) the controller drives between about −2 and +2.25 mA into the pump cell.
s: Check engine light
Sensor 3 value frozen near lambda 1 in live data
Downstream emission monitors not completed
c: Broken pump-current wire or pushed-back pin in the sensor plug
Sensor plug loose or not latched after exhaust work
Internal break in the pump cell of the probe

P2A39.d: P2A39 is set when the pump-current lead feeding the rearmost wide-band probe on bank 1 (sensor 3) is pulled below its permitted window, typically because the wire rubs through to chassis ground near the hot rear exhaust section. At ignition-on Saab's 2010 9-5 shows roughly 2.8 V on the pump-current pins of its front probe, so a reading near zero points to a ground short.
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Sensor 3 reading implausible or missing in live data
c: Pump-current wire chafed through to body or exhaust bracket
Internal short in the probe after thermal shock or water ingress
Faulty sensor interface in the engine control module

P2A3A.d: P2A3A means the voltage on the pump-current (positive control) lead of probe number three, bank 1, sits above its expected level. The usual culprit is contact with a supply: the heater feed runs in the same harness and connector, and moisture or heat damage at the plug can bridge the two.
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Sensor 3 reports an implausibly lean value
c: Pump-current wire touching the heater feed in harness or plug
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector under the car
Internal short between heater and pump cell of the probe

P2A3B.d: P2A3B points to a break in the negative current control line of wide-band sensor 3 on bank 1, the common return of pump and Nernst cell. Bosch calls it virtual ground (IPN/VM, pin 2 on the LSU 4.9), NTK names it COM; the controller holds it at a bias of about 2.5 V, as Saab's 2010 9-5 shows at the plug, so current can flow both ways.
s: Check engine light
Sensor 3 signal stuck around its mid voltage in live data
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor not completed
c: Broken virtual-ground wire or loose pin in the sensor plug
Corroded terminals in the connector near the rear exhaust
Internal break of the common electrode inside the probe

P2A3C.d: P2A3C is stored when the virtual-ground return belonging to the third probe of bank 1 falls below its intended bias. Because this line normally floats around 2.5 V rather than at chassis potential, a chafed wire touching the body or an exhaust bracket drags it down and leaves the pump cell little room to reverse its current, so rich mixtures can hardly be measured.
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Downstream emission monitors stay incomplete
c: Virtual-ground wire chafed through to chassis ground
Internal short from the common electrode to the sensor housing
Bias stage in the engine control module faulty

P2A3D.d: P2A3D flags the return line (virtual ground) of bank 1's sensor-3 wide-band probe as too high. Pulling this mid-level bias up to battery voltage usually takes a short to the heater supply, which shares the sensor plug, or water that has crept into a connector under the car.
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Sensor 3 lambda value rejected or shown as invalid
c: Virtual-ground wire shorted to the heater supply in harness or plug
Moisture bridging terminals in the sensor connector
Heater-to-electrode short inside a cracked probe

P2A3E.d: P2A3E is the alternative fuel version of P0148: the system cannot supply the gas or propane quantity the engine asks for. Ford had already defined its own code P1048 with this wording, listed with a lamp in the 2014 Boss 302S OBD table.
s: Hesitation or stalling on gas
Automatic switch to petrol
Lean fuel trim codes stored as well
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Gas or propane filter heavily restricted
Tank solenoid, rail solenoid or manual valve not fully open
Excess-flow valve on the tank tripped
Weak propane pump or pressure regulator not holding pressure
Tank pressure too low because the tank is nearly empty

P2A3F.d: On a bi-fuel or gas-start vehicle the control unit only changes over to gas once preconditions are met, for example warm coolant, enough pressure in the rail and a selected gas mode. P2A3F means this changeover did not happen within the calibrated time.
s: Vehicle keeps running on petrol much longer than usual
Gas indicator stays off or flashes
Check engine light, depending on calibration
c: Coolant warms up too slowly (thermostat stuck open, temperature sensor wrong)
Tank pressure too low for the switch-over
Regulator or vaporizer not heated enough by engine coolant
Tank or rail solenoid opening late or not at all

P2A40.d: P2A40 reports that fuel is passing through an injector into a rail where it does not belong. The term fits dual-fuel direct injection, where one injector carries both diesel and gas: Caterpillar's patent US9422899B2 explains that the diesel is kept at a pressure equal to or a little above the gas to seal the gas needle, so liquid seeping into the nozzle space on the gas side is expected, and a check valve plus a purg
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or operation on a single fuel
Rough running or smoke after a cold start
c: Worn internal seal or needle guide in a dual-fuel injector
Check valve between injector and gas rail leaking
Pressure difference between liquid and gas rail out of tolerance
Rail pressure sensor drifting and simulating a leak

P2A41.d: Some multi-tank CNG installations give a second cylinder, tank B, its own pressure transducer, so the module knows the remaining gas per tank and can check that the tank valve responds. P2A41 is the general electrical fault of that sensor, set when the circuit is faulty without a clear verdict of low or high.
s: Check engine light
Gas gauge wrong or showing empty
Tank B possibly no longer used
c: Plug at the tank B sensor loose, corroded or harness damaged
5 V reference or sensor ground disturbed

P2A42.d: Unlike its electrical siblings, P2A42 deals with a tank B pressure reading that is electrically valid but makes no sense. Examples: the value does not fall while gas is drawn from tank B, it stays frozen after refuelling, or it differs clearly from the pressure of the other cylinders after a long stop, when all tanks connected to one fill line should settle at about the same level.
s: Check engine light
Gas gauge implausible after refuelling or driving
Reduced range on gas
c: Tank B pressure sensor drifting or stuck
Tank B solenoid stuck closed or manual valve shut
Contact resistance in the sensor connector shifting the signal

P2A43.d: P2A43 is stored when the signal of the tank B pressure sensor drops below its lower electrical limit, a level that no real tank pressure produces. The usual reasons are a signal wire grounded against the frame, a missing 5 V reference or an internal short in the sensor.
s: Check engine light
Gauge drops to empty for tank B
Less usable gas range
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor
Internal short in the tank B sensor

P2A44.d: The counterpart to P2A43: the voltage on the tank B pressure sensor signal sits above its valid range. TransEco, for the tank A sensor of its gas conversions, names an open sensor or a short to power as the cause of the High code, which matches the usual pull-up layout of such inputs where a broken signal or ground wire drives the reading upward.
s: Check engine light
Gauge stuck at full for tank B
Stumbling when tank B actually runs empty
c: Sensor ground or signal wire open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

P2A45.d: P2A45 completes the tank B pressure group with the case that the other codes miss: the signal is mostly fine but jumps or drops out for moments, faster than any real gas pressure could change. Typical culprits are a plug that loses contact on rough roads, a wire rubbed through along the frame rail or a sensor with a cracked solder joint.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Gas gauge flickering or jumping
Occasional unexpected switch to petrol on bi-fuel vehicles
c: Tank B sensor plug with loose or corroded contacts
Harness chafed along frame or gas line
Intermittent internal fault in the sensor

P2A46.d: Larger CNG installations, for instance on trucks or buses, may carry three or more cylinders. Where a third one, tank C, has its own pressure transducer, P2A46 reports a general electrical fault in that sensor's circuit, stored when the module finds the signal unusable but cannot classify it as too low or too high.
s: Check engine light
Remaining gas shown wrongly
Tank C may be left unused
c: Wiring or plug at the tank C sensor damaged, loose or wet
Shared 5 V supply or sensor ground disturbed

P2A47.d: P2A47 is not about broken wires: the tank C sensor delivers a voltage inside its window, yet the pressure it reports cannot be true. Plausible tests are a value that stays flat while the engine draws gas from tank C, one that does not rise during filling, or a clear gap to tanks A and B after a long rest, since cylinders on a common fill manifold settle to similar pressure.
s: Check engine light
Gas level shown does not match refuelling or consumption
Shorter driving range on gas
c: Tank C sensor drifted or frozen at one value
Tank C solenoid not opening or manual valve closed

P2A48.d: With P2A48 the voltage from the tank C pressure sensor has fallen beneath the lowest value a working sensor ever outputs, even with the cylinder empty. In such three-wire circuits a low reading points to the signal line touching ground, a dead 5 V supply or a short inside the transducer.
s: Check engine light
Tank C reported empty despite being filled
Less gas range than expected
c: Signal wire of the tank C sensor touching ground
5 V reference open or shorted by another sensor on the same line
Internal short in the tank C transducer

P2A49.d: P2A49 is the mirror image of P2A48: the tank C pressure signal sits above the band a healthy sensor uses, so the module rejects it. In TransEco's AFCM table the tank A equivalent traces back to a sensor with an open circuit or a short to the supply.
s: Check engine light
Gauge for tank C stays at full
Hesitation once tank C really runs low
c: Ground or signal wire of the tank C sensor interrupted
Signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

P2A4A.d: Unlike P2A48 or P2A49, which describe a signal stuck out of range, P2A4A covers a tank C pressure value that flickers: brief spikes, gaps or steps that no gas cylinder could produce, since pressure in a large tank changes only slowly. Vibration is the usual trigger, acting on a connector with weak pin tension, a cable clip that has let go, or water creeping past a seal near the back of the vehicle, where tank C often
s: Check engine light appearing occasionally
Gas gauge jumps while driving
No noticeable effect between dropouts
c: Connector pins at the tank C sensor with weak contact
Water ingress at a connector seal

P2A4B.d: Gaseous fuel changes density with temperature, so gas systems measure it to meter the right mass; Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks, for example, use a thermistor at the rail for that density calculation and only switch to gas once both temperature and pressure allow it. The title of P2A4B names no location, which sets it apart from the tank temperature codes (P01AA ff.), the rail temperature codes (P01B4 ff.) and the v
s: Check engine light
Bi-fuel vehicle stays on petrol or switches back
Rougher running on gas
c: Plug or wiring of the gas temperature sensor faulty
Input stage or data link of the gas module disturbed

P2A4C.d: Here the gas temperature reading is electrically valid but implausible. A typical check compares it with other temperatures after a long cold soak, when gas, intake air and coolant should agree within a few degrees; another looks for the cooling that expansion in the regulator causes under heavy gas flow.
s: Check engine light after a drive cycle
Fuel trim off while running on gas
Often no noticeable driving issue
c: Sensor drifted, slow or stuck at one value
Sensor seated loosely or with poor thermal contact

P2A4D.d: P2A4D means the voltage of the gas temperature sensor is below its valid limit. Gas temperature sensors are normally NTC thermistors whose resistance drops as they warm up, so a low voltage would correspond to extremely hot gas; in practice it nearly always means the signal wire is grounded or the sensor is shorted inside.
s: Check engine light
Gas mode refused, bi-fuel vehicle runs on petrol
Live data shows an implausibly hot gas temperature
c: Signal wire of the gas temperature sensor shorted to ground

P2A4E.d: The counterpart to P2A4D: the gas temperature signal rises above its upper limit. With the usual NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, that equals an absurdly cold reading, and the most frequent reason is an open circuit, either a broken wire, a loose terminal or a sensor that has gone open inside.
s: Check engine light
Live data shows gas temperature at its coldest limit
Bi-fuel vehicle falls back to petrol
c: Broken wire or loose terminal in the sensor circuit
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P2A4F.d: Temperature changes slowly, so a gas temperature reading that leaps by tens of degrees within moments is not physics but wiring. P2A4F is set for such spikes and dropouts of the gas temperature signal, while P2A4D and P2A4E cover signals that stay out of range.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Short switches to petrol on bi-fuel vehicles
Jumping gas temperature in live data
c: Fretting corrosion or loose terminal at the sensor plug
Wire broken inside its insulation near the regulator

P2A50.d: A vaporizer, often called reducer or converter on LPG systems, turns liquid gas into vapour with heat taken from the engine coolant. The sensor in P2A50 sits on the outlet side of vaporizer A and tells the control unit whether that unit is warm enough.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Vehicle stays on petrol or switches back from gas
Gas mode indicator flashes or stays off
c: Plug or wiring of the vaporizer A outlet sensor faulty
Outlet temperature sensor of vaporizer A defective
Input stage of the gas control module disturbed

P2A51.d: P2A51 does not point to a broken wire: the outlet temperature of vaporizer A is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state. Typical tests compare it with coolant and ambient after a long stop, expect it to climb as the engine warms up, and expect a dip when heavy gas flow draws heat out of the unit.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Late or no switch-over to gas after a cold start
Uneven running or hesitation on gas
c: Sensor drifts or sticks at one value
Sensor badly seated or mounted at an unsuitable point
Vaporizer A really too cold (low coolant, air in the circuit, stuck thermostat)

P2A52.d: Temperature sensors of this type are usually thermistors whose resistance falls as they get warmer, the same principle Ford describes for the fuel rail sensor of its 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks. A signal under the lower limit would therefore mean an impossibly hot vaporizer A; in practice the signal line touches ground or the sensor is shorted inside.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode blocked, vehicle runs on petrol
Live data shows an implausibly hot vaporizer
c: Moisture or coolant in the connector

P2A53.d: P2A53 is the opposite case: the voltage of the vaporizer A outlet sensor sits near the supply reference, which a thermistor input reads as extreme cold. A broken wire, an unplugged or corroded connector, an open sensor element or a short to a voltage source all produce this.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
No switch-over to gas, bi-fuel vehicle stays on petrol
Live data shows a vaporizer far below freezing
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P2A54.d: A vaporizer full of coolant has a lot of thermal mass, so its outlet temperature can only change gradually. P2A54 is set when the vaporizer A signal jumps, drops out briefly or flickers in a way no real temperature could; the fault may be gone by the time a technician looks.
s: Intermittent check engine light, depending on calibration
Occasional switching back to petrol
Jumping vaporizer temperature in live data
c: Wire chafing on a hose or bracket
Sensor with an internal loose contact

P2A55.d: A second vaporizer appears where one heat exchanger cannot supply enough gas, for instance on large or heavy-duty engines. On LNG trucks the job is harder still: Westport's patent CA2862664C starts from liquid near −160 °C, heats it with engine coolant and places a gas temperature sensor downstream of the exchanger to choose how the coolant flows.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Reduced power or gas mode limited
Fall-back to the second fuel on dual-fuel engines
c: Plug or harness of the vaporizer B sensor damaged
Fault in the sensor input of the control module

P2A56.d: With two vaporizers fed by the same coolant, their outlet temperatures should behave alike, which gives the module a natural cross-check. P2A56 means the vaporizer B reading is electrically fine but out of line with that expectation, with the engine state or with its own history.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Power drop under high load on gas
Clear temperature gap between vaporizer A and B in live data
c: Vaporizer B sensor reads off or sluggishly
Vaporizer B gets too little coolant (air lock, kinked or blocked hose)
Sensor seated loosely in its port

P2A57.d: P2A57 sets when the outlet sensor on vaporizer B pulls its signal below the lowest valid voltage. On a thermistor that loses resistance with heat, as in the Ford CNG rail sensor, this would mean extreme heat, so the realistic causes are a signal lead grounded against the chassis and an internally shorted sensor.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation limited or switched off
Vaporizer B shown far hotter than vaporizer A
c: Signal lead of the B sensor grounded
Insulation worn through on a long harness run

P2A58.d: Here the signal of the vaporizer B outlet sensor rests at or near the reference voltage, so the module would see a deep-frozen unit. Typical reasons are an open wire, a plug that has backed out, a sensor element that has failed open or a short to a supply line.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas delivery reduced or fall-back fuel used
Vaporizer B shown at an impossibly low temperature
c: Open wire or plug of the B sensor backed out
Signal lead touching a supply line

P2A59.d: On heavy vehicles the gas hardware sees constant shaking, and long harness runs to the vaporizers add connectors that can loosen. P2A59 records that the vaporizer B outlet signal changed faster or more erratically than real temperature can, or kept dropping out for short moments.
s: Check engine light comes and goes, depending on calibration
Sporadic switching to petrol
Flickering gas indicator
c: Connector of the B sensor loose or corroded
Harness damaged by vibration or strain

P2A5A.d: Vaporizer C is the third unit in a gas system that splits the conversion of liquid fuel over several heat exchangers, a layout that only makes sense for engines with very high gas demand. Each unit needs its own outlet sensor because a vaporizer that cannot keep up shows it first by a falling outlet temperature; patent US6755643B2 even uses an outlet sensor to shut a vaporizer down once the draw exceeds its capacity.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation limited, less power at high load
Vehicle falls back to the other fuel
c: Connector or wiring of the vaporizer C sensor faulty
Control module input for sensor C faulty

P2A5B.d: With three outlet sensors in one system, a plausibility check can use a majority: if A and B agree and C stands apart, vaporizer C or its sensor is the odd one out. P2A5B means the C value is electrically valid but fails such a comparison or does not follow warm-up and load as it should.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Power loss at full load on gas
Vaporizer C differs clearly from A and B in live data
c: Sensor C stuck, drifting or slow
Vaporizer C genuinely too cold from lack of coolant or fouling

P2A5C.d: P2A5C stands for a vaporizer C outlet signal below the valid range. Since such inputs are normally NTC thermistors, the module would read an implausibly hot unit; a signal lead touching ground or a sensor shorted internally is far more likely.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation blocked or limited
Vaporizer C shown far too hot
c: Signal lead of sensor C shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector

P2A5D.d: P2A5D says the vaporizer C sensor signal is stuck high, near the reference voltage, which reads as extreme cold. An interrupted wire, a disconnected or corroded plug, an open sensor or a short to battery voltage are the candidates.
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode held back or output reduced
Vaporizer C shown at extreme cold
c: Wire to sensor C interrupted or plug disconnected
Signal lead shorted to battery voltage

P2A5E.d: P2A5E marks an unsteady vaporizer C signal: brief dropouts, spikes or a jagged trace that a coolant-heated part cannot really produce. The fault often clears itself and returns, so it matters what conditions trigger it.
s: Check engine light now and then, depending on calibration
Gas operation drops out occasionally
Spiky vaporizer C trace in recorded data
c: Connector of sensor C without firm grip
Contact pin pushed back in the housing

P2A5F.d: How the content of a second gas tank is measured depends on the fuel. CNG has no liquid surface, so the level is worked out from pressure, often corrected by tank temperature; GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel shows full near 3,600 psi and empty near 400 psi.
s: Check engine light
Gauge ignores the content of tank B
Range estimate on gas too low
c: Plug or wiring of the tank B sender faulty
Tank B level sender or Hall module defective
Reading module or data link to the engine module disturbed

P2A60.d: P2A60 flags a tank B level that is electrically valid but does not behave like a real fuel quantity: it fails to drop while gas is used from tank B, does not climb after filling, or swings wildly although the tank is at rest. Roush documents the stuck logic for its propane primary sender as P25B0, set when the value stays put over a considerable distance.
s: Check engine light after several trips
Gas gauge does not move as fuel is used
Unexpected running out of gas
c: Float arm in tank B bent or jammed (LPG)
Pressure or temperature input behind the calculated level drifting (CNG)
Contact resistance shifting the sender signal

P2A61.d: P2A61 is stored when the tank B level signal falls below the smallest voltage the sender produces even with the tank empty. Roush's manual for its dual-tank propane trucks names a sender wire shorted to ground or a damaged sender as causes of the low case and adds that the second-tank code P2067 leaves only the primary tank on the gauge.
s: Check engine light
Tank B shown empty or left out of the gauge
Shorter displayed gas range
c: Sender signal wire of tank B shorted to ground
Supply voltage of a Hall-type sender missing

P2A62.d: P2A62 is set when the tank B level signal climbs above the highest voltage a working sender delivers at full. For its dual-tank propane trucks Roush blames the high case on a disconnected sender or a wire shorted to more than 5 V, and with the second-tank code P2068 the gauge again falls back to the primary tank only.
s: Check engine light
Gauge shows only the primary tank
Content of tank B unknown to the driver
c: Tank B sender unplugged or wire open
Signal wire shorted to a voltage above 5 V

P2A63.d: Fuel slosh makes any level reading wobble a little, and modules filter that out. P2A63 goes further: the tank B level signal drops out or jumps in steps no filter can explain, then returns to normal.
s: Gas gauge for tank B jumps or briefly drops
Check engine light from time to time
Range display unsteady
c: Corroded contacts at the tank B sender from road spray
Cable pinched by a tank strap
Worn wiper track or loose Hall module in the sender

P2A64.d: A third gas tank, C, may have its own level input, either a real float sender in an LPG vessel or, on CNG, a value the module derives from that tank's pressure, the way Ford's 2003 bi-fuel trucks turned tank pressure into a gauge reading. P2A64 reports that the tank C level circuit is faulty without saying whether the signal is too low or too high; P2A66 and P2A67 make that distinction.
s: Check engine light
Gauge or range leaves out tank C
Otherwise normal driving
c: Long harness run to tank C damaged or plug loose
Fault in the tank C pressure input the level is derived from (CNG)

P2A65.d: For tank C this code reports a level that stays within the valid voltage window yet contradicts what happens to the tank. Examples are a reading that remains unchanged over many kilometres although tank C supplies the engine, no rise after a fill, or a level that disagrees with the pressure in a CNG cylinder.
s: Check engine light after several trips
Level for tank C frozen or illogical
Range estimate unreliable
c: Float in tank C sticking or sender mounted at a wrong angle (LPG)
Pressure or temperature input of tank C drifting (CNG)
Contact resistance shifting the level signal

P2A66.d: P2A66 says the tank C level signal is below its lower electrical bound. With voltage-output senders that typically comes from a signal wire grounded somewhere along its route, a sender shorted inside, or a missing supply to a ratiometric Hall module such as those Rochester builds for LPG vessels, which needs a few volts to produce any output.
s: Check engine light
Tank C displayed as empty
Refuelling earlier than needed
c: Tank C sender signal wire grounded
No supply voltage at a Hall-type sender

P2A67.d: P2A67 is the high-side partner of P2A66: the tank C level voltage lies above anything a correctly working sender outputs at full. An unplugged connector, a broken signal or ground wire and a short to a supply voltage all push the input there.
s: Check engine light
Tank C missing from the gauge
Driver unsure about remaining gas
c: Tank C sender plug loose or knocked off
Signal shorted to a supply voltage

P2A68.d: The last code of this block covers a tank C level signal that flickers: it is valid most of the time but suffers short gaps or jumps unrelated to fuel movement. On vehicles with three tanks the wiring to tank C is often the longest and has the most joints, each a chance for a loose crimp or green corrosion; frame flex can open a fractured conductor for an instant.
s: Tank C level jumps on the display
Check engine light now and then
Range display unsteady
c: Loose crimp or corroded joint in the long tank C harness
Conductor fractured, opening under frame flex
Unsteady tank C pressure input behind a calculated level (CNG)

P2A69.d: On a gaseous-fuel engine, the rail pressure regulator takes gas straight from the storage cylinders and steps it down for the injector rail. P2A69 covers the transducer on the high-pressure side of that regulator, set when its circuit is faulty without a clear low or high verdict.
s: Check engine light on
Gas mode not available, bi-fuel vehicle stays on petrol
Gas gauge implausible or showing empty
c: Connector or harness at the regulator damaged by heat, vibration or corrosion
Inlet pressure transducer on the regulator faulty
5 V reference or sensor ground disturbed
Engine or alternative fuel control module faulty

P2A6A.d: P2A6A flags a regulator inlet pressure reading that is electrically valid but implausible. Upstream of the regulator the value should fall slowly as gas is burned, jump after refuelling and, with the engine at rest, roughly equal cylinder pressure.
s: Check engine light on
Gas gauge does not match the actual fill level
Unexpected switch to petrol or gas mode refused
c: Inlet pressure transducer drifted or contaminated by oil carried in the gas
Manual or solenoid tank valve closed, so the reading does not change
Contact resistance in connector shifts the signal

P2A6B.d: P2A6B is stored when the signal voltage of the regulator inlet pressure sensor drops below its valid band. With a typical three-wire transducer (5 V feed, signal, ground) that means a signal lead shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a failed sensor element.
s: Check engine light on
Gas gauge shows empty although the tank is full
Gas mode refused, bi-fuel vehicle runs on petrol
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor on the same feed

P2A6C.d: P2A6C means the regulator inlet pressure signal sits above its plausible voltage ceiling. Typical causes are a signal wire touching a 5 V or battery-voltage circuit, an open sensor ground, an open signal line that the module pulls up internally (depending on its design), or an internal transducer fault.
s: Check engine light on
Gas gauge stuck at full regardless of consumption
Gas mode blocked, bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol
c: Sensor ground open or connector terminal pushed out
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage

P2A6D.d: P2A6D is the dropout code of the regulator inlet pressure sensor: the signal jumps or briefly vanishes, but not long enough for a steady low or high verdict. The regulator normally lives in the engine bay, next to the right-hand strut mount on GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel, and Blackstone requires warm engine coolant to circulate through its SAN209 unit so that it does not ice up.
s: Check engine light on, sometimes clearing again
Gas gauge flickers or jumps
Sporadic switch from gas to petrol while driving
c: Loose or widened terminal in the sensor connector
Condensation or corrosion in the plug near the coolant-heated regulator
Harness rubbing on hoses or brackets with intermittent contact

P2A6E.d: P2A6E is not a wiring fault: the inlet pressure sensor works, but the gas reaching the regulator is too weak for it to hold rail pressure. A regulator can only reduce pressure, so once the supply approaches its outlet setpoint, rail pressure sinks with it.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or stumbling in gas mode, especially at high load
Automatic switch to petrol or engine stalls on dedicated gas engines
c: Tank solenoid or manual shut-off valve not fully open
High-pressure filter clogged or line restricted
Inlet pressure sensor reading too low within its range

P2A6F.d: P2A6F reports a regulator inlet pressure above the calibrated maximum. Only cylinder pressure is present upstream of the regulator, so a genuinely high value usually comes from the tank side, such as overfilling at a dispenser without temperature compensation or a cold-filled cylinder that later warms up strongly; a transducer reading high but still in range is the other option.
s: Check engine light on
Gas mode blocked as a precaution
Often appears right after refuelling
c: Inlet pressure sensor reading too high within its range
Cylinder overfilled or strongly warmed after a cold fill
Sensor or calibration not matching the installed cylinder pressure rating

P2A70.d: Some heavy-duty LNG systems do not drive the cryogenic tank pump directly but through hydraulics: an engine- or motor-driven hydraulic pump supplies oil to a reciprocating hydraulic drive on each tank pump. Westport's patent US8726785B2 shows two LNG vessels whose pumps sit inside the tanks, plus a selector valve that the controller switches to decide which pump receives hydraulic flow.
s: Check engine light on
Fuel drawn from one LNG tank only, range reduced
Loss of gas supply, dual-fuel engine falls back to diesel-only or derates
c: Damaged harness or connector at the select valve on the frame
Output stage in the controlling module faulty

P2A71.d: P2A71 concerns the function of the hydraulic fuel pump select valve rather than its wiring: the circuit is intact, but the system does not respond as expected after a switch command. In Westport's design the controller links the hydraulic pressure it measures to whichever pump the selector valve should be feeding; if the pressure pattern does not match the commanded pump, or the empty-tank logic sees no change after
s: Check engine light on
Tank changeover does not happen or happens late
Uneven LNG levels between tanks
c: Valve spool sticking due to contaminated hydraulic oil
Worn valve leaking internally, flow reaches both pumps
Solenoid force too low, for example from low supply voltage

P2A72.d: P2A72 is set when the control circuit of the hydraulic fuel pump select valve reads lower than expected for the commanded state. On a low-side driver this typically means the control wire is shorted to ground, so the valve coil may stay energised; on a high-side driver a short to ground or a shorted coil pulls the output down and may trip its protection.
s: Check engine light on
Select valve stays switched, one tank pump runs permanently
Gas supply interrupted when the active tank runs empty
c: Control wire chafed on the frame and shorted to ground
Select valve coil with shorted turns
Water in the connector bridging to ground

P2A73.d: P2A73 signals that the select valve control circuit sits at a higher voltage than the commanded state allows. Typical faults are an open coil or broken wire on a low-side driven valve, which leaves the line at supply voltage, or a short to battery voltage that the output cannot pull down.
s: Check engine light on
Second LNG tank not used, range clearly shorter
Gas supply stops although fuel remains
c: Valve coil or control wire open
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Corroded connector pins with very high resistance

P2A74.d: P2A74 covers brief, recurring faults in the select valve control circuit that clear before a firm low or high verdict. On LNG trucks the valve usually sits near the tank-mounted pump and hydraulic lines, where frame flex, road spray and very cold surfaces around the cryogenic tank stress connectors and insulation.
s: Check engine light on, may go out again
Brief hesitation or pressure dips in gas mode
Irregular tank changeover
c: Loose terminal in the select valve connector
Moisture or ice in the connector near the cryogenic tank
Harness chafed along the frame rail with intermittent contact

P2A75.d: In a hydraulically driven LNG pump system the controller watches the oil pressure delivered by the hydraulic pump. Westport's patent US8726785B2 places this sensor in the supply line between the hydraulic pump outlet and the hydraulic drive, using it for three jobs: reversing the drive at each stroke end, spotting an empty tank when peak pressure stays low, and flagging leaks or other abnormal conditions.
s: Check engine light on
LNG pump stops or strokes irregularly, gas pressure drops
Dual-fuel engine runs on diesel only or with reduced power
c: Connector or harness at the hydraulic pressure sensor damaged

P2A76.d: P2A76 is set when the hydraulic pump pressure reading looks electrically sound yet makes no sense for the operating state. Westport's patent explains why a fixed expectation is not enough: pressure rises with hydraulic pump speed, which follows engine speed when the pump is engine-driven, and with the LNG pressure the cryogenic pump works against.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven LNG pressure or slow pressure build-up
Empty-tank warning although LNG remains
c: Low hydraulic oil level or external leak
Worn hydraulic pump or drive seals

P2A77.d: P2A77 is set when the signal from the hydraulic pump pressure sensor drops below the range a working sensor can deliver, typically because the signal wire or the 5 V reference is shorted to ground or the reference feed is open. On hydraulically driven LNG pumps this matters more than a mere missing value: Westport's patent US8726785B2 treats a peak hydraulic pressure that repeatedly stays low as the sign of an empty
s: Warning lamp with false empty-tank indication
Unexpected switching between LNG tanks
Gas supply stopped or reduced engine power
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled to ground

P2A78.d: P2A78 indicates that the hydraulic pump pressure sensor reports a voltage above its plausible maximum, as happens when the signal line touches the reference or battery voltage or the sensor ground is open. A false high reading is critical for the pump cycle, because rising oil pressure is the usual cue that a stroke has ended: Caterpillar's patent US9228574B2 names this as the conventional way to reverse the drive.
s: Warning lamp and very short or no pump strokes
Falling gas pressure and loss of power
Engine switches to reduced power or stops on gas
c: Sensor ground open or corroded at the connector
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor failed with output at full scale

P2A79.d: P2A79 records a hydraulic pump pressure signal that jumps or drops out for short moments without staying low or high long enough for P2A77 or P2A78. In a reciprocating LNG pump the controller reads this sensor continuously to find each stroke end, so a single spike can be mistaken for the end of travel and a brief dropout for a missing pressure peak.
s: Uneven fuel pressure or surging power on gas
Sporadic warning lamp that clears again
Occasional false empty-tank message
c: Loose or fractured crimp terminal in the sensor circuit
Moisture or ice in the sensor plug
Harness damaged by vibration at the hydraulic unit

P2A7A.d: P2A7A is the general circuit fault of the alternative fuel hydraulic pressure sensor, a measuring point that the code list keeps apart from the hydraulic pump pressure sensor of P2A75. Where it sits is not defined publicly, and no manufacturer documents the split.
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced LNG delivery or power limitation
c: Damaged connector or harness at the hydraulic sensor
Fault in a sensor reference or ground shared with other sensors

P2A7B.d: P2A7B covers a hydraulic pressure signal that is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state. Plausibility can be judged because pressures in the hydraulic drive of an LNG pump follow a known pattern: during a stroke the working side carries load pressure, while the return side stays close to reservoir level until the valve reverses.
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Irregular pump strokes or reduced power on gas
c: Sensor port blocked by contaminated oil
Restricted return line or filter raising return pressure

P2A7C.d: P2A7C is set when the hydraulic pressure sensor signal falls below its valid band, most often from a signal wire grounded against the chassis, an open 5 V reference or a sensor with an internal short. If this sensor watches the return side, as in one of Caterpillar's layouts, a dead-low reading would hardly stand out at first, since return pressure is low anyway; the range check against the minimum voltage still catc
s: Warning lamp on
Pump stops or delivers less LNG
Additional sensor codes if the reference is shared
c: Signal wire grounded against chassis or hydraulic lines
Open 5 V reference to the sensor

P2A7D.d: P2A7D means the hydraulic pressure sensor reads above its upper limit, typically because the signal line is touches the reference or battery supply, or its ground connection is broken. Unlike P2A7C, this fault is obvious at once: a full-scale reading while the pump is idle or retracting contradicts every other input.
s: Warning lamp on
Erratic or stopped pump strokes
Reduced power on gas
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal line shorted to reference or battery voltage

P2A7E.d: P2A7E flags a hydraulic pressure sensor signal that breaks up or spikes briefly, then recovers before the low or high checks of P2A7C and P2A7D mature. Pressure in a pump drive pulses with every stroke anyway, so the controller has to tell genuine pressure swings from electrical noise; what it treats as erratic is a change faster than the hydraulics can produce, or a signal vanishing between strokes.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Uneven pump cycling or brief power dips
c: Loose terminal in the sensor connector
Condensation or ice near the cryogenic tank

P2A7F.d: Hydraulically driven LNG pumps use solenoid valves to admit high-pressure oil to the drive side for the compression stroke and to vent it again for refilling. Caterpillar's patent US10060421B2 gives each of its six pumping elements, other counts being possible, a solenoid pilot that moves a spool between fill and drain positions; the controller sets timing and length of every stroke this way.
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced LNG delivery and lower power
Gas pressure drops under load
c: Open wire or loose connector at valve A
Solenoid coil of valve A burnt open
Output stage in the control module faulty

P2A80.d: P2A80 concerns the compression stroke valve of pump A when its circuit is intact but the outcome of a command does not match. In the patented multi-element design, the time the solenoid holds the spool in the fill position sets the stroke, and a shorter command yields a partial stroke; the controller therefore expects a defined gain in gas pressure or hydraulic load per activation.
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Uneven gas pressure and slight power loss
c: Spool of valve A sticking or slow
Weak return spring in the valve

P2A81.d: P2A81 is stored when the control circuit of pump A's compression stroke valve sits lower than the commanded state allows. With a low-side driver this mostly points to the control wire touching ground, which can energise the solenoid permanently; with a high-side driver a coil with shorted turns or a grounded feed pulls the output down until its protection trips.
s: Warning lamp on
Pump A stops delivering, power drops at high load
c: Control wire of valve A shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the solenoid coil

P2A82.d: P2A82 shows the drive line to pump A's compression stroke valve at a higher level than the commanded state permits, most likely because the coil winding or its wire is broken where the valve is switched to ground, or because the line touches battery voltage and the output stage loses control of it. The solenoid then cannot move the spool into the fill position, so oil never reaches the drive side and pump A performs
s: Warning lamp on
Falling gas pressure and power loss
Engine may stall on gas with a single pump element
c: Open coil or broken wire at valve A
Control wire shorted to battery voltage

P2A83.d: P2A83 reports an open or otherwise faulty control circuit at the compression stroke valve of alternative fuel pump B. Whether a second pump exists depends on the layout: in Westport's patent US8726785B2, two LNG vessels each carry their own hydraulically driven pump, while Caterpillar's multi-element pump splits one unit into several separately switched elements.
s: Warning lamp on
LNG in one tank cannot be used
Reduced power under high load
c: Open wire or loose connector at valve B
Solenoid coil of valve B open
Output stage for valve B faulty

P2A84.d: P2A84 is set when pump B's compression stroke valve is electrically sound yet the pump does not respond as commanded. A controller that drives several pumps or elements in turn can compare them: in Caterpillar's multi-element patent, flow results from how often the elements are fired and how long each waits, so an element adding less pressure per command than its neighbours stands out.
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Lower delivery from one tank or element
c: Spool of valve B slow or leaking internally
Worn plunger seals on the cryogenic side of pump B

P2A85.d: P2A85 means the drive output for pump B's compression stroke valve reads too low for its commanded state. Typical are a control wire chafed through to the frame, which can keep the solenoid energised even when the controller wants it off, or a coil with shorted windings that draws excessive current.
s: Warning lamp on
Pump B delivers nothing, reduced power or range
c: Control wire of valve B chafed through to the frame
Coil of valve B with shorted windings
Output stage for valve B shorted

P2A86.d: P2A86 is stored when pump B's compression stroke valve circuit shows a higher voltage than its state allows, pointing to an interrupted coil, a broken return wire where the valve is switched on the ground side, or a short to the supply. The valve then rests in its drain position: drive oil bypasses pump B and its plunger stays retracted.
s: Warning lamp on
One LNG tank is no longer emptied
Shorter range on gas
c: Open coil or broken wire at valve B
Control wire shorted to supply voltage
Corroded terminals in the valve B plug

P2A87.d: P2A87 covers the control circuit of the compression stroke valve on alternative fuel pump C, reporting an open or otherwise unusable circuit. A third pump valve only exists on systems with at least three separately switched pumping units.
s: Warning lamp on
Uneven gas pressure, slight power loss at high load
c: Open wire or loose connector at valve C
Solenoid coil of valve C open
Output stage for valve C faulty

P2A88.d: P2A88 reports that the compression stroke valve of pump C works electrically but its effect does not match the command. In a sequenced multi-element pump, each activation should add a similar amount of pressure to the gas accumulator or rail; an element that keeps falling short, or whose share fluctuates, stands out against its neighbours.
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Little noticeable change in driving
c: Deposits making the spool of valve C open late
Partly blocked oil passage to element C
Worn cryogenic seals on element C

P2A89.d: P2A89 is set when the drive circuit of pump C's compression stroke valve reads low for the commanded state. Most often the control wire has found a path to ground, so the solenoid may stay on, or the coil has shorted turns and pushes the output stage into current limiting.
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced power at high load
c: Control wire of valve C shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the coil of valve C

P2A8A.d: P2A8A indicates that pump C's compression stroke valve circuit sits higher than the commanded state allows, from an open coil, a broken wire or a short to the supply rail. The solenoid cannot shift the spool, which stays in the drain position, and element C never starts a compression stroke.
s: Warning lamp on
Uneven gas pressure at high load
c: Open coil or broken wire at valve C
Fault in the supply or ground shared by the pump valves
Control wire shorted to the supply rail

P2A8B.d: P2A8B means vaporizer A is not doing its job well enough, rather than reporting a wiring fault. On LPG engines this unit, also called reducer or converter, draws engine coolant heat to turn liquid gas into vapour at a steady pressure.
s: Check engine or gas warning lamp on
System stays on petrol longer after a cold start or falls back to petrol under load
Hesitation, rough running or stalling after coasting on gas
Frost or condensation on the vaporizer body
c: Too little coolant reaching vaporizer A (air lock, kinked hose, thermostat stuck open)
Worn diaphragm or seat in the pressure stage of vaporizer A
Oily residues from the gas clogging the vaporizer chambers
Outlet temperature sensor reading wrong but still within range

P2A8C.d: P2A8C flags vaporizer B as underperforming: the gas leaving it is colder, or less completely vaporized, than the module expects for the current flow. With LNG the temperature gap is extreme, and Westport's patent CA2862664C describes the typical failure.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Reduced power or gas mode blocked, especially when cold
Ice on the vaporizer or gas lines behind it
c: Coolant partly frozen inside vaporizer B after cold start or long idling
Valve that switches between parallel and counter flow stuck
Low coolant level or too little antifreeze in the mixture
Deposits reducing heat transfer in vaporizer B

P2A8D.d: P2A8D concerns a third vaporizer, found where large engines or several fuel branches need more heat exchange than one or two units provide. The code means unit C turns too little liquid into usable gas, or delivers it too cold, while its outlet sensor works.
s: Warning lamp on, often with little noticeable change in driving
Loss of power at high load when all vaporizers are needed
One vaporizer housing noticeably colder than the others
c: Coolant branch to vaporizer C restricted or unbalanced against A and B
Fouled heat exchange passages in vaporizer C
Pressure stage of vaporizer C sticking or leaking internally
Outlet sensor of C drifting so that the comparison fails

P2A8E.d: P2A8E reports that alternative fuel pump A no longer delivers what it should, a mechanical or hydraulic fault rather than an electrical one. Such pumps move liquid fuel, typically LNG out of a cryogenic tank.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Power loss at high load, gas pressure sagging
Pump runs noticeably longer to refill the accumulator
