Engine switched to reduced output or diesel-only operation
c: Worn dynamic piston seals in pump A
Leaking inlet or outlet check valve of pump A
Hydraulic drive of pump A delivering too little force or speed
Impurities in the fuel passing the filter and damaging the pump

P2A8F.d: P2A8F applies to a second alternative fuel pump whose output has fallen short of expectations. Layouts with two pumps usually give each LNG vessel its own pump, a redundancy Westport's documents mention explicitly.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Usable range shorter, fuel left in one tank
System changes to the other tank earlier than usual
c: Worn seals reducing the delivery of pump B
Tank served by pump B almost empty, mimicking a weak pump
Broken drive shaft or coupling between hydraulic drive and pump B

P2A90.d: P2A90 marks pump C of the alternative fuel system as delivering too little. A third pump may belong to a further tank or, in Caterpillar's design US10060421B2, be one of several pumping elements driven in sequence.
s: Warning lamp on
Weak pull or hesitation shortly after a long stop
Gas pressure recovers slowly after heavy acceleration
c: Vapour at the inlet of pump C after warm soak, causing cavitation
Worn seals or valves in pump C
Clogged inlet strainer or filter ahead of pump C

P2A91.d: A tank select valve decides which storage vessel feeds the fuel system. That sets it apart from a tank shutoff valve (P224C, P2A22 and onward), which simply opens or isolates one cylinder, and from the hydraulic fuel pump select valve (P2A70 and onward), which routes drive oil to a pump.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Only one tank is used, range noticeably shorter
Fuel gauge shows content left although the engine runs short of gas
c: Loose connector or broken wire to select valve A
Burnt-out solenoid coil of valve A
Faulty output stage in the alternative fuel module

P2A92.d: P2A92 is the functional check for tank select valve A: the wiring tests pass, yet the fuel system does not behave as if the commanded vessel were connected. Software can judge this only through pressures.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tanks empty unevenly or in the wrong order
Short gas supply although one vessel still holds fuel
c: Select valve A sticking from dirt, ice or wear
Valve A leaking across its seat so both vessels are drawn
Tank pressure sensor giving a misleading reading

P2A93.d: P2A93 is stored when the module measures a voltage on the control line of tank select valve A that falls short of the level expected for the commanded state. With a low-side driver this usually means the line touches ground, which can energise the solenoid permanently and keep valve A in its switched position regardless of the command.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tank selection stuck, one vessel emptied completely
Fuse or output protection of the gas module trips
c: Control wire of valve A chafed through to ground
Condensation or water in the connector of valve A
Shorted turns in the coil of valve A

P2A94.d: P2A94 reports a control voltage at tank select valve A above what the module expects for the commanded state. On a valve switched to ground by the module, an open coil or broken lead leaves the line floating at supply voltage; alternatively a chafed wire contacts a battery feed that the output stage cannot pull down.
s: Malfunction lamp on
No change to the next tank, gas runs out early
Engine switches to its other fuel or reduced power
c: Open coil or broken lead on a ground-switched valve A
Control wire of valve A touching a battery feed
Corroded pins with high resistance at valve A

P2A95.d: P2A95 says the module finds no proper current path through tank select valve B. Where a second select valve exists, it typically serves the next vessel or supply in line.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Content of one vessel cannot be used
Range well below the usual figure
c: Loose plug or broken wire to select valve B
Open solenoid coil of valve B
Output stage for valve B in the module defective

P2A96.d: P2A96 is about tank select valve B working electrically but not doing what it is told. In an LNG layout like the one in Westport's US8726785B2, where one pump draws from either of two vessels through an insulated select valve, the module can verify the switch from the pump's behaviour: right after selecting a full vessel, the drive work per stroke should be normal, whereas a reading that stays low suggests the pump s
s: Malfunction lamp on
Gas supply drops right after a tank change
One vessel stays full while the other runs dry
c: Valve B held by ice or cold-hardened seals
Debris preventing valve B from shifting fully
Pump defect interpreted as a select valve problem

P2A97.d: P2A97 indicates that the drive line of tank select valve B reads too low. If the module feeds the valve from the positive side, a short to ground in the wire or a coil with shorted windings drags the output down, and the stage switches off to protect itself, so valve B falls back to its spring position.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tank change does not happen or happens at the wrong time
Gas mode ends early with fuel still on board
c: Wire to valve B chafed against a tank strap or bracket
Shorted windings in the coil of valve B
Moisture bridging the pins of the valve B plug

P2A98.d: P2A98 appears when the voltage on the control circuit of tank select valve B stays higher than the module allows for the commanded state. A ground-switched valve with an interrupted winding or lead shows this pattern, as does a wire that has picked up battery voltage.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Second vessel never used, gas runs out early
Gauge shows reserve while power drops
c: Interrupted winding or lead at valve B
Control line of valve B in contact with battery voltage
Corrosion at the valve B connector raising resistance

P2A99.d: P2A99 belongs to installations with at least three selectable vessels or supplies and reports an open or otherwise broken control circuit at select valve C. Published designs mostly show two vessels, such as Westport's LNG arrangement with one pump and a valve choosing the tank, or Cespira's pair of compressed-gas supplies; a third valve extends the same principle.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Third vessel stays full or is never isolated
Total range reduced
c: Disconnected plug or broken lead at select valve C
Coil of valve C burnt out
Module output for valve C failed

P2A9A.d: With P2A9A, select valve C passes its electrical tests, but the effect of switching does not show up as expected. The likely evidence is pressure: once vessel C is selected, its own tank pressure sensor should begin to fall with consumption and the pressure ahead of the regulator should match that vessel's level.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tank C level hardly changes over a tank cycle
Fault appears mainly in cold weather
c: Valve C not shifting fully because of wear or contamination
Internal leakage letting vessel C feed in the wrong position
Faulty tank C pressure reading misleading the check

P2A9B.d: P2A9B is logged when the control circuit of tank select valve C reads below the expected level. Common electrical findings are a lead grounded against the frame, a pinched wire under a tank strap or a coil with internal shorts.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Third tank used constantly or not at all
Unexpected tank changes during the drive
c: Lead of valve C grounded against the frame or pinched under a tank strap
Internal short in the coil of valve C
Water in the plug of valve C

P2A9C.d: P2A9C reports a control voltage at select valve C above the level the commanded state permits. The usual reasons are an interrupted coil or wire on a valve the module switches to ground, which leaves supply voltage on the line, or a foreign voltage fed in from a damaged neighbouring wire.
s: Malfunction lamp on
Third vessel never drawn, range reduced
Earlier change to the other fuel
c: Open coil or wire on ground-switched valve C
Foreign voltage from a damaged neighbouring wire

P2A9D.d: P2A9D points to a slow loss of gas from the high-pressure side, from the cylinders up to the regulator, too small to notice while driving. A Toyota and Denso patent, US6467466B1, explains the catch: with the valves open, a modest pressure drop cannot be told apart from consumption.
s: Malfunction or gas warning lamp on
Tank pressure noticeably lower after parking
Faint gas smell near the tanks or lines
Gas mode blocked at the next start on some systems
c: Seeping high-pressure fitting or loosened connection
Tank or shutoff valve not sealing fully when closed
Aged O-rings in the filter or regulator inlet
Drifting high-pressure sensor simulating a pressure loss

P2A9E.d: Liquid-phase propane and LPG systems pump more fuel to the rail than the injectors use; the surplus flows back to the tank and carries heat and vapor away with it. A return line valve opens or blocks that path.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Hard or long cranking on a warm engine, as vapor is not flushed out of the rail
Switch to the base fuel or reduced power on bi-fuel or dedicated systems
c: Corroded, wet or loose connector at the tank-mounted valve
Broken wire in the frame or tank harness
Open solenoid coil in the return valve
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the valve supply
Failed output stage in the fuel control module

P2A9F.d: P2A9F covers the grey zone between a clean open and a clean short: the control circuit of the return line valve is connected, but the current or voltage the output stage measures while driving it does not fit the command. Typical reasons are a coil whose resistance has drifted, a few shorted windings, or high contact resistance in a corroded connector that lets the coil pull in only weakly or late.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Occasional hard starts after a hot soak
Fault comes and goes with temperature or moisture
c: Solenoid coil resistance out of range or partially shorted windings
High contact resistance from corrosion or water in the connector
Low supply voltage at the valve from a weak relay contact or ground
Output stage of the fuel control module measuring incorrectly

P2AA0.d: P2AA0 means the module reads too low a voltage on the control line of the return line valve, which almost always points to a short to ground. What follows depends on which side the module switches.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Return valve stays open or the valve fuse blows, depending on the circuit layout
Irregular rail pressure or switch to the base fuel
c: Control wire chafed through and touching the frame or tank
Water in the valve connector bridging to ground
Internal short in the solenoid coil
Damaged output stage in the fuel control module

P2AA1.d: P2AA1 is the opposite electrical case to P2AA0: the valve drive wire sits at too high a voltage, usually because it touches a battery-fed wire. Where the module switches the ground side, as in the ROUSH CleanTech Gen 4 propane system with its relay-module ground, a line stuck at supply level leaves no voltage across the coil, so the valve cannot be energized at all and stays in its rest position.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Return valve cannot be switched and stays in its rest position
Poor hot starts or switch to the base fuel
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Solenoid winding shorted to its supply terminal
Bent or bridged pins in the valve connector
Output stage in the fuel control module shorted internally

P2AA2.d: P2AA2 is a hydraulic fault, not an electrical one: too little liquid fuel comes back from the rail to the tank. The return keeps the fuel in the rail cool and liquid, so a weak return lets it warm up and boil.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Hard starting or stalling after a hot soak from vapor in the rail
Hesitation or lean running under load
Switch to the base fuel or reduced power
c: Return valve or return check valve sticking closed
Kinked, crushed or clogged return line or filter
In-tank pump delivering too little, leaving no surplus to return
Faulty pressure regulator in the return path

P2AA3.d: P2AA3 belongs to the cold-start strategy (CSERS) newer diesels run in the first minutes after a long soak. CARB phases in from 2026 to 2028 that the OBD system must confirm, under defined monitoring conditions such as a soak of six hours or more, that the EGR valve and the EGR cooler bypass actually follow their cold-start setpoints by a clearly measurable amount, in the right direction and beyond normal start-up beh
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Higher NOx in the warm-up phase, possible inspection failure
c: EGR valve B sticking or slow from soot at low temperature
Faulty position sensor on EGR valve B misleading the control
Clogged EGR cooler or passage in loop B

P2AA4.d: P2AA4 is the mirror case of P2AA3: during the cold-start phase, EGR path B recirculates more exhaust than intended. Many calibrations deliberately keep EGR low in a cold engine, so a valve that leaks or hangs open is the classic cause.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle and smoke after a cold start
Stalling or hesitation while the engine is cold
c: EGR valve B leaking or stuck partly open from carbon
Position sensor offset making the valve open further than commanded
Intake or exhaust throttle fault raising the pressure difference across loop B

P2AA5.d: P2AA5 comes from the H-bridge that drives the DC motor of the bank 1 EGR cooler bypass flap: the driver chip itself reports that it is getting too hot. GM's diesel summary tables carry this monitor from 2017 (17OBDG04) to 2025 (25OBDG04A) as a motor overtemperature check.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bypass flap no longer driven, so warm-up EGR cooling stays at its last state
Possible further EGR or cooler efficiency codes
c: Bypass flap binding on soot or corrosion, motor working against resistance
Internal fault in the bypass actuator motor
Partial short between the motor wires
Overheating or faulty H-bridge in the engine control module

P2AA6.d: P2AA6 is the bank 2 version of the bypass driver protection code. It only exists on engines with a separate EGR cooler and bypass actuator for the second cylinder bank, typically V engines whose banks each have their own exhaust manifold feeding EGR.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 bypass flap stays in its last position
Possible NOx or EGR temperature codes for bank 2
c: Bank 2 bypass flap binding on soot or corrosion
Internal fault in the bank 2 actuator motor
Partial short in the bank 2 actuator wiring
Faulty driver stage in the engine control module

P2AA7.d: Thermal management modules on modern engines use motor-driven rotary valves to split coolant between radiator, heater, oil or transmission cooler and engine block. A position sensor reports each valve's angle so the module can regulate it in closed loop.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slow warm-up or reduced cabin heating
Fluctuating or elevated coolant temperature reading
c: Loose, corroded or coolant-wetted connector, or damaged sensor wiring
Lost 5 V supply or ground to the position sensor
Failed position sensor inside the valve module
Faulty sensor input in the engine control module

P2AA8.d: With P2AA8 the position sensor of coolant valve B delivers an electrically valid signal, but its content is implausible: it sticks while the motor turns the valve, jumps by more than a real valve could move, or lies outside the end stops the module learned. A worn sensor track, a magnet that has shifted on the valve shaft or a slipping gear between motor and sensor are typical findings.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine warms up slowly or runs hotter than usual
Heater output varies
c: Worn or contaminated position sensor in the valve module
Slipping gear or shifted magnet between valve shaft and sensor
Intermittent contact in the connector causing signal jumps
Learned end stops lost after a module or valve replacement

P2AA9.d: P2AA9 is set once the position sensor on coolant valve B reports a value below its valid band, which nearly always means the signal wire or the sensor output is pulled toward ground. Rotary coolant valves in thermal management modules report their angle so the engine computer can steer coolant between radiator, heater and other loops.
s: Check engine light on
Engine warms up slowly or runs cooler than usual
Cabin heating or transmission warm-up weaker, depending on what valve B serves
c: Sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Position sensor electronics in the valve module failed (often only as complete valve unit)
Coolant or moisture in the sensor connector creating a leakage path to ground

P2AAA.d: With P2AAA the position sensor of coolant valve B reports a value above anything a working sensor would deliver. Typical reasons are a signal line touching a supply wire, a damaged output stage inside the sensor or, depending on how the input is wired, an interrupted ground.
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature swings or stays off target
Possibly reduced engine power if the module protects against overheating
c: Signal wire in contact with a supply or reference voltage wire
Sensor ground open at the connector or splice
Position sensor in the valve module defective

P2AAB.d: P2AAB covers a position signal from coolant valve B that is valid most of the time but drops out, jumps or flickers for short moments. Such patterns usually come from a contact that opens under vibration or heat, a lead that rubs against hot engine parts, or interference on the digital sensor line.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Occasional temperature swings without a steady pattern
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Widened or loose terminal in the valve connector
Harness rubbing on hot or moving engine parts
Electrical interference or poor ground on the sensor line

P2AAC.d: P2AAC is the general circuit fault of a sensor meant to recognise diesel where only gasoline belongs, so the system can react to misfuelling before damage occurs. No manufacturer documents this sensor or the code publicly, and its exact design is not described in sources available.
s: Check engine light on
Misfuelling warning unavailable or shown without reason
Usually no change in how the engine runs
c: Corroded or loose connector at the sensor near the tank or fuel line

P2AAD.d: P2AAD means the diesel presence sensor delivers an electrically valid signal whose content does not make sense: it may report diesel although no refuelling has taken place, never change at all, or contradict other information the engine computer has about the fuel. No manufacturer documents this code or its test publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Unjustified misfuelling message, or a real misfuelling going unnoticed
c: Sensing element coated with deposits or residues
Calibration of the plausibility check not suited to the fuel quality in use

P2AAE.d: P2AAE is stored when the diesel presence sensor signal falls below the lowest value the input accepts, which points to a short to ground on the signal line or a sensor whose output has collapsed. Whether a low reading would otherwise stand for diesel or for gasoline is not published, so the code says nothing about the fuel in the tank, only that the reading cannot be used.
s: Check engine light on
Misfuelling protection inactive
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, often chafed on the underbody
Sensor supply or reference voltage missing

P2AAF.d: P2AAF reports the diesel presence sensor signal stuck above its upper limit. Common reasons are a signal wire touching a battery-fed line, an open ground or signal path that lets an internal pull-up drive the input high, or a sensor with a failed output stage.
s: Check engine light on
Misfuelling warning unreliable
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Open sensor ground or signal wire

P2AB0.d: P2AB0 concerns the electronics of the particulate matter sensor rather than its sensing element: the sensor control unit, which feeds the electrodes, measures their current and reports over CAN, finds an internal error in its own measuring path. GM's 2025 diesel tables (25OBDG04A and B) describe it as an internal fault of the current switcher: the electrode current read in the small range must lie between a minimum a
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter monitoring cannot complete
Driving behaviour usually unchanged
c: Internal fault in the PM sensor control unit (sensor and control unit usually replaced as one part)
CAN wiring fault that older sensor versions also report as P2AB0
Unstable supply or ground at the sensor control unit

P2AB1.d: P2AB1 reports that the control module of an electrically heated catalyst does not work as it should, for example because its self-test fails or the heating it delivers does not match the demand. Such heaters bring a catalyst to working temperature right after start or in low-load driving.
s: Check engine light on
Higher emissions after cold start; inspection may fail
Driving behaviour largely unchanged
c: Internal fault in the heater control module (power stage or self-test)
Module software fault, update may be available
Module overheated due to poor cooling or high ambient heat at its mounting

P2AB2.d: P2AB2 points to the power feed of the catalyst heater control module: the voltage it measures at its own supply input lies outside the window in which it may switch the heater. That window matters because these heaters draw several kilowatts; Vitesco's demonstration vehicle used a 4 kW disc, fed in 48-volt mild hybrids from energy recovered while braking, as DieselNet reports.
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst heating not available, higher emissions after cold start
Further voltage-related fault codes possible
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the heater supply
Corroded or loose ground or high-current terminal
Weak 48-volt battery or faulty DC/DC converter in mild-hybrid systems

P2AB3.d: P2AB3 is part of the cold-start component checks that CARB phases in for 20, 50 and 100 percent of new vehicles in 2026, 2027 and 2028. Right after a start that follows a long standstill, charge motion, runner and swirl valves must follow the cold-start command clearly, toward the target and further than they would at a start without that strategy.
s: Check engine light on
Rougher idle in the first minutes after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions, otherwise often unnoticed
c: Actuator or vacuum unit too weak to move the flaps when cold
Flap shaft stiff from carbon or oil deposits
Linkage detached or broken between actuator and shaft

P2AB4.d: P2AB4 is the bank 2 version of the open-stuck check during cold start, so it only appears on engines with a separate runner control for each cylinder bank, typically V or flat engines. The runner flaps of the second bank fail to leave their open position as long as the cold-start routine runs, so that bank burns its mixture with less charge motion than intended.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running between the banks shortly after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions
c: Leaking vacuum line or diaphragm on the bank 2 actuator
Bank 2 flap shaft stiff from deposits

P2AB5.d: P2AB5 is the opposite of P2AB3: during cold start the runner control on bank 1 remains in its closed position and does not follow a command to open. CARB requires, for 2026 to 2028 phase-in vehicles, that such valves react measurably and in the commanded direction while the cold-start conditions hold, meaning a soak of six hours or more and coolant close to ambient.
s: Check engine light on
Less power in the first minutes after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions
c: Flaps stuck closed by deposits or condensate freezing at low temperature
Actuator motor or vacuum valve does not move the shaft
Broken return spring or worn shaft bushing

P2AB6.d: P2AB6 reports the runner flaps of bank 2 held in the closed position during the cold-start phase, against a command to open them. Like its siblings it exists only on engines that control each bank's runners separately and only becomes testable after a soak of six hours or more at ambient temperatures from -6.7 °C upward, as defined in CARB's cold-start rules.
s: Check engine light on
Slightly uneven running and reduced pull after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions
c: Bank 2 flaps seized by deposits or ice
Bank 2 actuator or its control valve defective
Shared actuator supply or vacuum source weak (often with P2AB5)

P2AB7.d: P2AB7 is the general circuit fault for the position sensor on wastegate A, found on engines whose wastegate is moved by an electric motor rather than a vacuum can. Turbo A is the first one in the exhaust flow on series layouts or the bank 1 unit on parallel layouts.
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable lack of power, boost limited
Often stored together with P0299 or the stuck wastegate codes P25B3/P25B4
c: Electric wastegate actuator failed, e-clip missing or actuator rod damaged (sensor sits in the actuator)
Chafed harness or loose connector near the hot turbocharger
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (reflash available for some models)

P2AB8.d: P2AB8 means the wastegate A position signal has fallen below its valid floor, which points to a short to ground, an open signal or reference wire, or a dead sensor. GM's 2019 tables for the 2.7L L3B read the sensor as a percentage of its reference and fail below 5 % in 30 of 38 samples taken every 100 ms; the 2025 tables use below 1 % in 10 of 12.
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Reduced power because boost control is restricted
May appear together with P0245 when a shared harness section is damaged
c: Sensor harness pinched or chafed between turbocharger and intake hose (short to ground)
Open reference or signal wire, or pushed-out terminal in the actuator connector
Position sensor inside the electric actuator failed

P2AB9.d: P2AB9 is logged when the wastegate A position signal climbs above its valid ceiling. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, an open ground return that lets the input float upward, or an internal sensor fault.
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Lower power under load, boost held back
Powertrain fault (wrench) indicator on some Ford models
c: Signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Position sensor inside the electric actuator failed

P2ABA.d: P2ABA covers a general circuit fault of the position sensor on the wastegate of turbocharger B, so it can only occur on engines with two turbos and electric wastegates: on a parallel layout the turbo of bank 2, on a series layout the second one downstream. Ford uses it on twin-turbo EcoBoost V6 engines.
s: Check engine light, on Ford also the powertrain (wrench) indicator
Reduced power, boost limited
c: PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Damaged harness or connector at the bank 2 turbocharger
Electric wastegate actuator B with its built-in position sensor failed

P2ABB.d: P2ABB reports that the position signal of the turbocharger B wastegate is too low, as a short to ground, a broken signal or supply wire or a failed sensor would cause. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary applies the same window as for turbo A and sets the code below 0.50 V after 4 s.
s: Check engine light
Less power, especially when accelerating hard
c: Sensor wire chafed to ground near the bank 2 turbocharger
Open reference supply or signal wire, loose connector
Position sensor in wastegate actuator B failed

P2ABC.d: P2ABC is the high-voltage fault on the wastegate B position sensor: according to Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary the input sits above 4.50 V for 4 s, a picture typical of a signal line shorted to the reference supply or an open sensor ground. On the 2.7L F-150 of model years 2021-22 Ford blames false P2ABC entries on calibration and fixes them by reprogramming the PCM (TSB 22-2357); TSB 23-2353 and SSM 54083 add it f
s: Check engine light, on Ford possibly the wrench indicator
Reduced power under load
c: PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Open sensor ground or heat-damaged terminal at the actuator
Signal wire shorted to the reference supply or battery voltage

P2ABD.d: P2ABD is raised by the output stage that powers the electric wastegate actuator of turbocharger A when it detects excessive current or overheating. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary groups it with P0243 in the wastegate A circuit check: the PCM's smart driver chip recognises a short to battery or ground and an open load on its own and reports within 0.4 s, and the stuck open/closed tests P25B3/P25B4 are only allowed wh
s: Check engine light on
Clearly reduced power because the wastegate is no longer driven
Stuck wastegate checks P25B3/P25B4 not run while the code is stored
c: Wastegate flap or rod binding from soot, corrosion or heat so the motor stalls
Actuator supply wires chafed to ground or to each other
Driver stage in the PCM faulty

P2ABE.d: P2ABE is the turbo B counterpart of P2ABD: the output stage driving the second electric wastegate actuator signals overcurrent or thermal overload. It therefore applies only to twin-turbo engines with two electric actuators, such as Ford's EcoBoost V6.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, uneven boost between the two banks
c: Wastegate B rod or flap seized by corrosion or heat
Shorted winding in electric actuator B
Actuator harness pinched against the turbocharger

P2ABF.d: P2ABF points to an open circuit in the reference voltage line of the intake air oxygen sensor on bank 1. This sensor is a wide-band element placed in the intake tract, usually before the intercooler, that measures how much oxygen the incoming charge still contains and therefore how much exhaust has been recirculated.
s: Check engine light on
EGR runs without sensor feedback or is reduced, higher NOx emissions
c: Broken reference wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Corroded or loose sensor connector in the damp intake area
Sensing cell of the intake oxygen sensor internally open

P2AC0.d: P2AC0 is set when the reference voltage circuit of the bank 1 intake air oxygen sensor is electrically present but behaves implausibly, for example drifting or not matching what the ECM expects for the current EGR and pressure state. Stellantis documents it explicitly for the 2.0L turbo four (sales code EC2) of the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio: TSB 18-067-22 REV.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Engine software that detects the fault falsely (Stellantis reflash for Giulia/Stelvio 2.0L)
Intake oxygen sensor aged or contaminated by oil mist from crankcase ventilation
High resistance in the reference wire or connector

P2AC1.d: P2AC1 flags a reference voltage below the range the ECM accepts on the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor. This usually means the reference lead is shorted to ground or the sensing cell inside the sensor has broken down.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or uncontrolled, possibly higher NOx and a failed emissions test
c: Reference wire chafed through to ground
Sensing cell of the intake oxygen sensor broken down internally
Sensor interface in the ECM faulty

P2AC2.d: P2AC2 means the reference voltage at the intake oxygen sensor of bank 1 reads above its permitted range. A reference lead shorted to a supply wire or battery voltage in the harness, a lost ground on the sensor side or water in the connector are the usual triggers; a sensor with an internally damaged cell can produce the same picture.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx emissions may rise
c: Reference wire shorted to a supply or battery voltage wire
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector
Open ground on the sensor side

P2AC3.d: P2AC3 is the open circuit fault in the reference voltage lead of the intake air oxygen sensor assigned to bank 2. A second intake sensor only exists where each cylinder bank has its own intake or EGR path, for example on V engines with two separate charge air routes; engines with a single sensor use the bank 1 code P2ABF.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced or uncontrolled
c: Broken reference wire or loose terminal at the bank 2 sensor
Harness damaged by heat near the bank 2 turbocharger or exhaust
Sensing cell of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor internally open

P2AC4.d: P2AC4 marks an implausible but electrically intact reference voltage on the second-bank intake oxygen sensor. It is the bank 2 twin of P2AC0, which Stellantis documents for the four-cylinder Alfa Romeo 2.0L; an inline four with one intake path has no bank 2, so P2AC4 would only appear on engines fitted with a second intake sensor.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Bank 2 intake oxygen sensor aged or contaminated by crankcase vapours
Calibration that judges the signal too strictly
High resistance in the reference wire or connector

P2AC5.d: P2AC5 reports that the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor sees a reference voltage below the permitted limit, typically a short to ground in the reference lead or a breakdown of the sensing cell. No manufacturer publishes this code, and engines with a separate intake oxygen sensor for bank 2 are rare.
s: Check engine light on
Higher NOx, possibly a failed emissions test
c: Reference wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to ground
Shared sensor supply or ECM fault (if P2AC1 is present as well)

P2AC6.d: P2AC6 indicates an excessive reference voltage on the intake oxygen sensor serving bank 2, as happens when the reference wire touches a supply or battery feed, when the sensor ground is open or when moisture bridges the connector pins. Like the other bank 2 codes of this group, it is not documented by any manufacturer; the basis is CARB's general rule that input components must be checked for out-of-range values in b
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
c: Reference wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to a supply or battery feed
Moisture bridging pins in the connector

P2AC7.d: P2AC7 is the general circuit fault of the second coolant temperature sensor in the low-temperature loop that serves a water-cooled charge air cooler. Where two sensors exist, one usually sits at the cooler inlet and the other at its outlet, so the module can judge how much heat the cooler removes; in GM's 2025 diesel table, sensor A measures the water entering the cooler.
s: Check engine light on
Implausible or missing value for sensor B in live data
Reduced boost or power on some engines
c: Loose, corroded or coolant-contaminated sensor B connector
Chafed or broken wire between sensor B and the module
Faulty sensor input or reference in the engine control module

P2AC8.d: P2AC8 sets when charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B delivers an electrically valid value that makes no sense for the situation, for example after a long engine-off period when every temperature in the engine bay should have converged, or when it fails to change while the loop pump runs and the cooler heats up. No maker documents this exact check publicly; Ford and GM only publish thresholds for sensor A (P
s: Check engine light on, often only after several drives
Sensor B reads clearly different from sensor A after a cold soak
Higher intake air temperature under load
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in the low-temperature loop
Sensor B drifting out of its characteristic
Electric charge air cooler coolant pump weak or not running
Control module software needing an update

P2AC9.d: P2AC9 reports that the signal of charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B has dropped below its permitted window. These sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low signal stands for an implausibly hot coolant and usually means the signal wire touches ground or the element is internally shorted.
s: Check engine light on
Live data shows an extremely high coolant temperature for sensor B
Coolant pump of the loop runs constantly or boost is reduced
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Coolant in the connector bridging the terminals

P2ACA.d: P2ACA is the opposite end: the voltage from charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B sits above anything a real temperature would produce. For a thermistor input this looks like extreme cold and is typical of an unplugged connector, a broken signal wire, a lost sensor ground or a short to a voltage source.
s: Check engine light on
Live data shows an extremely low coolant temperature for sensor B
Reduced boost on some engines
c: Disconnected plug or broken signal wire of sensor B
Open ground or return line of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P2ACB.d: P2ACB covers a sensor B signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of following the slow temperature changes of a coolant loop. The title, without the word circuit, also includes erratic values while the wiring stays intact.
s: Check engine light comes and goes
Sensor B value jumps in live data
c: Terminal with weak contact tension in the sensor B plug
Harness rubbing through intermittently under vibration
Sensor B element with unstable output

P2ACC.d: P2ACC is the general circuit code for a second reductant (DEF) temperature sensor outside the tank; the tank sensors have their own series (P205A ff. and P2ADA ff.).
s: Check engine light and DEF/SCR warning
Countdown or speed limitation if the fault persists
c: Connector of sensor B corroded by DEF residue
Damaged wiring between sensor B and the controller

P2ACD.d: P2ACD flags a reductant temperature sensor B reading that is electrically fine but disagrees with the other temperatures the SCR controller knows, typically checked after a cold soak, when DEF lines, tank and ambient should read about the same. No manufacturer publicly describes P2ACD.
s: Check engine light after a cold start
SCR warning with no noticeable driving change
c: Controller software with an overly tight plausibility check
Sensor B drifting from its characteristic
Line heater warming the sensor area during the check

P2ACE.d: P2ACE means the signal of reductant temperature sensor B lies below its valid voltage band. With the NTC elements used for DEF temperature, a low voltage translates into an extremely hot reading, so a signal line rubbing through to ground, a crushed connector or DEF that has wicked into the plug and bridges the contacts are the usual suspects.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Implausibly high DEF temperature in live data
Frozen DEF lines in winter
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
DEF wicked into the connector bridging the terminals

P2ACF.d: P2ACF is set when reductant temperature sensor B reports a voltage above its valid band. For a thermistor that reads as deep cold, and it is what an open signal wire, a missing sensor ground, a disconnected plug or a short to supply voltage cause.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Implausibly low DEF temperature in live data
Delayed start of dosing after a cold start
c: Open signal wire or disconnected plug at sensor B
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage

P2AD0.d: P2AD0 stands for short interruptions or jumps in the signal of reductant temperature sensor B. The current title reads circuit intermittent only, without erratic.
s: Check engine light that appears sporadically
Jumping DEF temperature in live data
c: Moisture or DEF residue in the sensor B connector
Wire breaking intermittently inside the insulation

P2AD1.d: P2AD1 compares the voltages of position signals C and G and sets when they stop describing the same position. What the letters mean depends on the layout; GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 for an engine with two throttle bodies is the clearest public key: C is sensor 1 and G sensor 2 of the bank 2 throttle (P0227/P0228 and P212C/P212D), so C/G is the internal pair of that second throttle, the counterpart of the bank 1 pair A/
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limited throttle response
c: Raised contact resistance in the throttle connector
Worn or drifting sensor track in the second throttle body
Fault on the shared 5 V reference or sensor ground

P2AD2.d: P2AD2 sets when signals B and G no longer agree in voltage. On engines with one throttle body per bank this is a cross-bank comparison: with GM's 2023 letter scheme, B is the second track of the bank 1 throttle and G the second track of the bank 2 throttle.
s: Check engine light on
Possible loss of power
Further throttle codes such as P2135 or P2136 stored
c: High resistance at the pins of the throttle actuator connectors
Drifting position track in one of the throttle bodies
Damaged wiring to one throttle actuator

P2AD3.d: P2AD3 compares tracks A and G. In GM's 2023 scheme A is the first sensor of the bank 1 throttle body and G the second sensor of the bank 2 unit, so the pair links both throttles of a V engine and can reveal that one plate is not where the other suggests.
s: Check engine light on
Possible loss of power or emergency throttle mode
c: Raised contact resistance in the connectors of both throttle actuators
One throttle body with a faulty position sensor
Fault on a shared sensor supply or ground

P2AD4.d: P2AD4 reports that the voltage of an intermediate system, a supply level between the 12 V network and a high-voltage traction battery, has fallen below its lower limit. In practice this describes 48 V networks of mild hybrids, which carry a belt or integrated starter-generator and loads such as electric compressors; German makers agreed on such a level in 2011, and Audi and Mercedes-Benz use it since 2018.
s: Warning lamp or message about the electrical system
Start-stop and electric boost unavailable
Engine may not restart via the starter-generator
c: Weak or deeply discharged 48 V battery
Starter-generator not charging the intermediate network
DC/DC converter drawing the network down

P2AD5.d: P2AD5 is the high counterpart: the intermediate voltage level, in current vehicles mostly a 48 V mild-hybrid network, rises above its permitted maximum. Overvoltage typically arises when the starter-generator regenerates harder than the battery can accept, for example with a full or cold 48 V battery, a battery that has disconnected itself internally, or a faulty regulator in the generator or DC/DC converter.
s: Warning message about the electrical system
Recuperation, electric boost and start-stop unavailable
c: Starter-generator regulating the voltage too high
48 V battery disconnected internally or unable to accept charge
Faulty DC/DC converter feeding back into the network

P2AD6.d: P2AD6 is the general circuit code of the position sensor in the motor of the reductant (DEF) pump. Modern supply pumps often use a brushless motor whose rotor position must be known for commutation and speed control; a Cummins Emission Solutions patent names a Hall-effect rotor position sensor as one option and back-EMF evaluation as the sensorless alternative.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing stops; countdown to speed limitation
c: Position sensor or electronics inside the pump module defective
DEF residue or corrosion in the pump connector
Missing supply or ground for the pump electronics

P2AD7.d: P2AD7 sets when the motor position signal of the reductant pump is electrically valid but does not fit what the pump should be doing, for instance a rotor position or derived speed that is out of step with the commanded drive pattern. No maker documents P2AD7 publicly.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Pressure build-up of the DEF system fails, often after cold nights
c: Pump stiff or partly frozen, crystallised DEF in the pump head
Position sensor inside the pump giving a shifted signal

P2AD8.d: P2AD8 reports a reductant pump motor position signal stuck below its valid range. For Hall-type sensors this mostly means the output is pulled to ground permanently: a signal wire shorted to ground, a sensor that has lost its supply, or an internal short in the pump electronics.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF pump does not run, no dosing
c: Sensor supply missing, e.g. blown fuse or open feed
Internal short in the pump electronics

P2AD9.d: P2AD9 is the high-side fault: the pump motor position signal stays above its permitted range. An open signal line pulled up by the controller's internal resistor, a broken sensor ground or a short to the supply rail produce this picture.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
No DEF pressure build-up, dosing stops
c: Open signal line or broken sensor ground
DEF residue corroding the pump connector
Signal shorted to the supply rail

P2ADA.d: P2ADA checks whether the second DEF tank temperature reading is plausible. GM documents it twice.
s: Check engine light after a cold start
DEF or SCR warning message
c: DEF quality sensor with drifting temperature element
Chafed engine harness disturbing the signals

P2ADB.d: P2ADB flags a value from the second DEF tank temperature sensor that lies below the lowest temperature the sensor can physically report, so the controller treats it as a circuit fault and not as cold fluid. GM is the documented user.
s: Check engine light right after the fault is detected
DEF or SCR system warning in the cluster
Countdown to reduced power or restart lock if left unrepaired
c: Defective thermistor in the DEF quality or tank sensor unit
Moisture or DEF crystals in the sensor connector
Damaged signal or supply wiring to the tank sensor

P2ADC.d: P2ADC is the upper limit check on the same sensor B: the reported DEF temperature is higher than the fluid in the tank could ever get. In GM's 2017 and 2018 diesel calibrations the quality sensor thermistor has to exceed 155 °C in 40 of 50 samples, with cranking finished and more than 11 V at the powertrain relay; the outcome is a Type A code.
s: Check engine light on
DEF system message, often together with other harness-related codes
Possible inducement countdown toward reduced power
c: Internal fault in the quality sensor or smart tank sensor unit
Chafed engine harness disturbing the sensor circuit
Corroded or loose pins at the tank sensor connector

P2ADD.d: P2ADD judges how the sensor B signal moves over time instead of how high it is. Fluid in a tank warms and cools slowly, so sudden jumps suggest a loose contact or a failing element.
s: Check engine light that may return after clearing
Jumping DEF temperature in live data
DEF or SCR warning message
c: Loose or corroded contact at the tank sensor connector
Degrading thermistor in the quality or tank sensor unit

P2ADE.d: P2ADE is the general circuit code for reductant tank temperature sensor B, intended for systems that report a fault on this input without splitting it into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P2ADE publicly.
s: Check engine light on
DEF or SCR warning
Possible inducement countdown
c: Open signal line or unplugged tank sensor connector
Input fault in the SCR or engine control module

P2ADF.d: P2ADF means the engine control module has concluded that air reaches the cylinders of bank 2 without passing the air measurement. Audi documents the code for the 4.0 litre TFSI V8 in the A8, S8, SQ7, SQ8, RS Q8, RS 6 Avant and RS 7 from model years 2019 to 2023.
s: Check engine or exhaust warning light on
Whistling noise from the engine bay
Rough idle or misfire codes
c: Leaking full-load crankcase breather line on bank 2 (Audi 4.0 TFSI)
Split intake or boost hose on bank 2
Leaking intake manifold gasket on bank 2

P2AE0.d: P2AE0 says the calibration (trim) wire of bank 1's intake O2 sensor has lost continuity. On a Bosch-type wide-band element this is pin 5 (RT/IA), which connects a resistor in the plug that Bosch uses to set the characteristic of each individual sensor; without it the ECM scales the oxygen signal wrongly.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or run without oxygen feedback
NOx emissions may rise
c: Trim lead (pin 5) broken in the harness
Trim contact pushed back or corroded in the sensor plug
Calibration resistor inside the sensor connector open

P2AE1.d: P2AE1 is stored when the voltage on the trim circuit of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor falls below its window. With the ignition on, the 2010 Saab 9-5 expects roughly 2.8 V on terminal 5 of its wide-band probe, the trim connection; a value near zero suggests a lead rubbing on ground or a shorted resistor in the sensor plug.
s: Check engine light on
EGR cut back, possibly higher NOx
c: Trim lead chafed through to ground
Calibration resistor in the sensor plug shorted
Open trim lead on sensors whose interface reports it as low

P2AE2.d: P2AE2 means the voltage on the trim lead of the intake air O2 sensor for bank 1 is too high. In the six-wire harness of a wide-band probe this line runs next to the heater feed, so a pinched wire or moisture bridging the pins in the connector can drag it towards battery voltage.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx may rise
c: Trim lead touching the heater supply
Moisture bridging contacts in the sensor plug
Internal short in the sensor or its connector module

P2AE3.d: P2AE3 reports a break in the pumping current lead of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor, pin 1 of a Bosch LSU 4.9 (APE/IP). Through this wire the ECM drives current into the pump cell while the Nernst cell is kept on its set point; Ford's patent US9441564B2 explains that the size of that current reflects the oxygen share of the charge, from which the EGR dilution is calculated.
s: Check engine light on
EGR runs without sensor feedback or is switched off
c: Sensor plug loose or not latched
Pump cell inside the sensor open

P2AE4.d: P2AE4 flags too low a level in the pumping current circuit belonging to the bank 1 intake sensor, usually a pump lead chafed through to ground or an internal short in the pump cell. Saab's 2010 9-5 gives a useful reference for the same wire on its exhaust probe: about 2.8 V on terminal 1 at ignition-on with the sensor unplugged, and its low code P2238 sets when the signal stays under 1.7 V for 3 s on overrun.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or switched off
Possibly higher NOx at an emissions test
c: Pump current lead shorted to ground
Internal short in the pump cell
Sensor interface in the ECM faulty

P2AE5.d: P2AE5 is the high-side fault of the pumping current lead on the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor. A short to the heater supply or another battery feed in the harness is the classic cause; because the intake sensor works in damp air close to where blow-by gas and EGR enter, water in the plug comes next.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx may rise
c: Pump current lead shorted to the heater or another supply
Water or condensate in the sensor plug
Sensor interface in the ECM damaged by the short

P2AE6.d: P2AE6 points to an open negative current control line on the bank 1 intake air oxygen sensor. This is the shared return of pump and Nernst cell, which Bosch names virtual ground (IPN/VM, pin 2); Saab's 2010 9-5 shows about 2.5 V on it at ignition-on, a bias that lets the pump current change direction.
s: Check engine light on
EGR runs without oxygen feedback
c: Corroded or loose return contact in the plug
Internal break of the common electrode in the sensor

P2AE7.d: P2AE7 is set when the virtual-ground return of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor is pulled below its bias. In operation this lead sits roughly 2.5 V above chassis, as Saab's 2010 9-5 documents for its wide-band probe; a wire touching the engine block, a bracket or the intake pipe drags it towards zero.
s: Check engine light on
EGR cut back, possibly higher NOx
c: Return lead chafed against engine or bracket
Internal short of the common electrode to ground
Bias source in the ECM faulty

P2AE8.d: P2AE8 reports that, on bank 1's intake air oxygen sensor, the negative current control line sits above its intended level. For the bias on this return to climb towards battery voltage, something must feed it: most often the heater supply sharing the six-pin plug, sometimes condensate in a connector that collects moisture from the intake air.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx may rise
c: Return lead shorted to the heater supply
Internal short between heater and cell

P2AE9.d: P2AE9 is the bank 2 version of the open trim circuit: the line from the ECM to the calibration resistor of the second intake air oxygen sensor has no continuity. A separate sensor for bank 2 only makes sense where each cylinder bank draws its charge or EGR through its own path; nobody has published a vehicle that uses P2AE9.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced or without feedback
c: Trim contact pushed back in the plug
Trim lead broken, often near the hot exhaust of bank 2
Calibration resistor in the sensor connector open

P2AEA.d: P2AEA reports a trim circuit voltage below the permitted range at the bank 2 intake O2 sensor. Likely culprits are a trim wire grounded where the harness passes the second turbocharger, or a damaged resistor inside the sensor connector.
s: Check engine light on
Higher NOx, driveability usually unchanged
c: Trim lead grounded near the second turbocharger
Calibration resistor in the plug damaged
Fault in a ground or ECM path shared with bank 1

P2AEB.d: P2AEB indicates excessive voltage on the trim wire serving the second bank's intake O2 sensor. A short to the heater or another supply wire, or moisture bridging contacts in the plug, can lift the line; Saab's 2010 9-5 test procedure for the comparable exhaust probe expects roughly 2.8 V on its trim terminal at ignition-on, so a reading near battery voltage is a clear sign.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
c: Trim lead shorted to the heater or another supply
Moisture bridging contacts in the plug
Internal short in the sensor connector module

P2AEC.d: P2AEC means the pumping current wire of the second-bank intake oxygen sensor is interrupted. On a Bosch-style element the ECM uses this lead to push oxygen into or out of the measuring gap until the Nernst cell is balanced; the current needed is the oxygen signal.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 without feedback or switched off
c: Pump current lead broken, often from heat near bank 2 exhaust
Sensor plug loose or not latched
Pump cell inside the sensor open

P2AED.d: P2AED stands for a pumping current circuit on the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor that reads below its limit. A pump lead grounded on the engine or a breakdown inside the pump cell are the usual reasons.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 limited, possibly higher NOx
c: Pump current lead grounded on the engine
ECM sensor interface faulty (likely if bank 1 also reports)

P2AEE.d: P2AEE marks the pumping current lead of the bank 2 intake air oxygen sensor as too high. Contact with the heater feed in the shared plug, chafing against a live wire or water that has entered the connector can raise it.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
c: Pump current lead touching the heater feed
Harness chafed against a live wire

P2AEF.d: P2AEF indicates that the return line, or virtual ground, of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor is open. Both cells of a wide-band element reference this lead, pin 2 (IPN/VM) on the Bosch LSU 4.9, which the ECM biases so current can flow both ways.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Internal break of the common electrode

P2AF0.d: P2AF0 is stored when the negative current control circuit of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor falls below its window. Because the return is meant to sit at a bias of roughly 2.5 V, which Saab's 2010 9-5 lists as the test value on terminal 2 of its exhaust probe, any path to chassis ground pulls it down: insulation worn through at a clip, a crushed connector or an internal short in the sensor.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 cut back, possibly higher NOx
c: Return lead worn through at a clip or bracket
Internal short of the sensor to ground

P2AF1.d: P2AF1 is the high-side fault of the virtual-ground return on the bank 2 intake air oxygen sensor. Lifting this biased line towards supply voltage requires contact with a feed, most often the heater circuit in the same plug, or condensed water inside a connector.
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise
c: Return lead shorted to the heater circuit
Bias source in the ECM faulty

P2AF2.d: P2AF2 reports an open or otherwise faulty control line for a third starter relay. Such a relay appears where cranking is split across several switching stages, for instance on stop-start engines.
s: Stop-start function disabled
Occasional or permanent no-crank
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Broken control wire or unplugged relay connector
Blown fuse or missing supply to the relay coil
Faulty output driver in the control module

P2AF3.d: P2AF3 sets when the control line of starter relay C is pulled toward ground at a moment the module expects a different level. What that does to the relay depends on the driver type: with ground-side switching the short acts like a permanent on command, with supply-side switching the coil never gets current.
s: Stop-start inoperative
Relay energised all the time or not at all, depending on circuit design
Possible no-crank
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Faulty output driver in the control module

P2AF4.d: P2AF4 points to a control wire of starter relay C that carries battery voltage when the module has switched its driver off, typically because it touches a 12 V feed or because the driver leaks. With supply-side switching that can keep the coil energised; with ground-side switching the module can no longer pull the relay in.
s: Stop-start disabled
Relay may stay engaged with ignition off
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V circuit
Water in the relay socket or power distribution box

P2AF5.d: P2AF5 means starter relay C remains in its energised state when it should have dropped out. Stellantis uses it as Starter Relay 3 Stuck On for the power control relay of its dual-battery stop-start system: Jeep Grand Cherokee 2021 to 2025, Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer 2022 to 2025, RAM 1500 2025, and earlier Pacifica, Durango, Compass, Wrangler and Gladiator.
s: No crank or no start
Stop-start inoperative, service message for the system
Auxiliary battery not being charged
c: Loose or corroded B+ connection at main or auxiliary battery
Depleted auxiliary battery causing a false fail
Open or poorly seated 150 A fuse or fuse array

P2AF6.d: P2AF6 is the reverse fault on relay C: commanded to switch, the relay does not change state. Stellantis names it Starter Relay 3 Stuck Off, on some Wagoneers Dual Starter Relay Stuck.
s: Check engine light on
Stop-start disabled
Occasional failure to restart after an auto-stop
c: Power distribution centre connector not fully seated
Depleted auxiliary battery causing a false fail

P2AF7.d: P2AF7 is the open-circuit or general fault on the control line of a fourth starter relay, relay D. Four separately monitored starter relays only make sense where there is more than one cranking path, for example a pinion relay, a second starter or a battery isolation stage on a stop-start engine.
s: Auto-stop not available
Intermittent no-crank
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Broken control wire or corroded connector
Blown fuse feeding the relay coil

P2AF8.d: P2AF8 is logged when the control line of starter relay D shows a short to ground. Depending on whether the module switches the coil on its ground side or its supply side, the relay then either sits permanently energised or can no longer be operated.
s: No start or no crank
Several unrelated electrical faults at the same time
Stop-start unavailable
c: Spread or bent terminals in the power distribution centre connector

P2AF9.d: P2AF9 indicates that the control line of starter relay D sits at supply voltage although the driver is switched off, mostly a short to a 12 V circuit or a leaking driver stage. With ground-side switching the module can then no longer energise the coil, because both coil ends see battery voltage; with supply-side switching the coil may stay energised and keep a cranking path live, which is the more critical case for s
s: Stop-start disabled
Starter may not engage, or in rare cases keep running
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Control wire chafed against a live circuit
Leaking output driver in the control module

P2AFA.d: P2AFA describes starter relay D staying engaged although the control module has commanded it to release; the module infers this from a feedback signal, a voltage or current that should have changed. No manufacturer documents P2AFA publicly.
s: Starter keeps turning or grinding after the engine starts
Stop-start disabled
Battery drain while parked
c: Control wire receiving voltage from another circuit

P2AFB.d: P2AFB is set when starter relay D ignores an on command: the module energises it, but the expected change of voltage or current in the switched circuit never appears. No manufacturer documents P2AFB publicly.
s: Engine does not crank on the affected path
Auto-stop permanently unavailable
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Low supply voltage or poor ground at the relay
Loose connector at the relay or distribution box

P2AFC.d: P2AFC is the general circuit code for a fourth engine coolant temperature sensor. Engines with split cooling, electric pumps or separate head, block, radiator and heater circuits carry several such sensors, and how they are numbered is up to each maker.
s: Check engine light on
Cooling fans running more than usual on substitute value
Thermal management in default mode
c: Open wire or loose connector at sensor 4
Faulty input stage in the engine control module

P2AFD.d: P2AFD flags a sensor 4 coolant reading that stays inside the electrical limits but makes no sense, for instance a value that disagrees with the engine's other temperature readings once everything has cooled down for hours, or that hardly moves while the engine warms up. CARB requires such rationality checks for coolant temperature inputs used by emission controls.
s: Check engine light, often only after a cold start
Sensor 4 value clearly differing from the others in live data
c: Corrosion adding resistance in the connector
Air pocket at the sensor after coolant service

P2AFE.d: Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors, so a signal from sensor 4 that is too low stands for an impossibly hot reading, usually a signal wire grounded or a shorted element. GM documents P2AFE for the 2.7 L turbo four (L3B) in its 2019 tables: the configurable temperature input system sets it when the resistance of the sensor 4 channel drops below about 41 Ω, corresponding to 150 °C, for 5 s within a 6 s window; Type B,
s: Check engine light after two trips
Cooling fans running at full speed
Implausibly high coolant temperature in live data
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, for example by harness chafing
Faulty input in the engine control module

P2AFF.d: P2AFF reports an excessive sensor 4 signal. For an NTC thermistor that means an implausibly cold reading, mostly from an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a line shorted to voltage.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Implausibly cold coolant temperature in live data
Thermal management running on a default value
c: Open signal wire or unplugged connector
